objectives.statement: Sketch and describe the graphs of $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$ and $y=\tan x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$, including period, amplitude and key features.
Use the symmetry of the sine and cosine graphs to find a second solution of a trigonometric equation on $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$.
Solve trigonometric equations of the form $\sin x=k$, $\cos x=k$ and $\tan x=k$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
Model a real periodic context (such as height above ground) with a trigonometric expression and solve for a given value.

prerequisites.statement: Find an acute angle from $\sin,\cos$ or $\tan$ using a calculator's inverse functions (from Lesson 6.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The 'first' solution found by a calculator's inverse function is always the starting point from which every other solution on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ is generated using symmetry.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise the exact trigonometric values and how $\sin,\cos,\tan$ relate to a right-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.4).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The CAST diagram and the graphs extend the SAME three ratios beyond $90^{\circ}$; without a solid right-triangle picture of what $\sin,\cos,\tan$ mean, the extension to a full circle/graph has nothing to build on.

prerequisites.statement: Read coordinates and key features (intercepts, turning points, period) from a sketched graph.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The sine, cosine and tangent graphs are read and sketched using exactly this same graph vocabulary.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a simple linear equation, including one with a negative coefficient (e.g. $6-5c=9\Rightarrow c=-0.6$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several equations in this lesson must first be rearranged algebraically into the form $\sin x=k$ or $\tan x=k$ before the graph/CAST method can be applied.

diagnostic_items.question: A calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(0.6)=36.87^{\circ}$. Is this the ONLY angle between $0^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$ with sine equal to $0.6$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. Sine is also positive in the second quadrant, so $180^{\circ}-36.87^{\circ}=143.13^{\circ}$ is a second solution.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because the calculator gave one definite answer.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats the calculator's single principal-value output as the complete solution set, missing that most trig equations on a full range have more than one valid solution.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Directly targets whether the learner knows a calculator's inverse trig function returns only ONE of possibly several solutions on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch the sine graph from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$ and mark both points where the curve crosses the horizontal line $y=0.6$.

diagnostic_items.question: Is $\cos200^{\circ}$ positive or negative?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Negative: $200^{\circ}$ is in the third quadrant, where only tangent is positive.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Positive, since cosine is 'usually positive'.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Does not use the quadrant/CAST picture at all, instead guessing a sign based on a vague overall impression of cosine rather than checking which quadrant $200^{\circ}$ falls into.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner can determine a sign using the CAST quadrant rule rather than guessing, which is essential before attempting to solve any equation with multiple solutions.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Draw the four quadrants of the CAST diagram, locate $200^{\circ}$ in quadrant 3, and read off that only tangent is positive there.

diagnostic_items.question: If $\tan x=2.5$ and the calculator gives $x=68.2^{\circ}$, what is the SECOND solution between $0^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $68.2^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=248.2^{\circ}$ (tangent repeats every $180^{\circ}$, in quadrants 1 and 3).

common_wrong_answers.answer: $360^{\circ}-68.2^{\circ}=291.8^{\circ}$, using the sine/cosine symmetry rule instead of the tangent one.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Applies the wrong symmetry rule (the one that correctly finds a second sine or cosine solution) to a tangent equation, instead of adding $180^{\circ}$ as tangent's own period requires.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner distinguishes the symmetry rule for tangent (add $180^{\circ}$) from the different rules used for sine ($180^{\circ}-x$) and cosine ($360^{\circ}-x$).
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch the tangent graph from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$ and mark the repeating pattern every $180^{\circ}$ explicitly.

diagnostic_items.question: What is the period of $y=\sin x$, and what is its maximum value?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Period $360^{\circ}$; maximum value $1$ (reached at $x=90^{\circ}$).

common_wrong_answers.answer: Period $180^{\circ}$, confusing it with the tangent graph's period, or maximum value stated as some number other than $1$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Mixes up the period of sine/cosine ($360^{\circ}$) with the shorter period of tangent ($180^{\circ}$), or has not fixed in memory that sine/cosine oscillate strictly between $-1$ and $1$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Confirms basic graph vocabulary (period, maximum) is attached correctly to the sine graph before building CAST/equation-solving on top of it.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch $y=\sin x$ from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$, labelling the maximum, minimum and the point where the curve returns to its starting value.

theory_blocks.title: Trigonometry beyond the triangle
theory_blocks.body: So far, $\sin,\cos,\tan$ have only been used for ANGLES INSIDE A RIGHT-ANGLED TRIANGLE, so between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. But a calculator will happily compute $\sin200^{\circ}$ or $\cos315^{\circ}$ too. These values come from rotating a point around a circle, and plotting them against the angle produces [[blue:smooth, repeating wave-shaped graphs]] — the key to solving equations with MORE THAN ONE solution.

theory_blocks.title: Where the values come from: the unit circle
theory_blocks.body:
Every value of $\sin$, $\cos$ and $\tan$ — not only those for an angle inside a triangle — comes from one picture. Draw a circle of radius $1$ centred on the origin, measure the angle $x$ anticlockwise from the positive horizontal axis, and mark the point $P$ where that rotation lands.

For an angle between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$, drop a perpendicular from $P$: the right-angled triangle formed has hypotenuse $1$, so its horizontal side is $1\times\cos x$ and its vertical side is $1\times\sin x$. The coordinates of $P$ ARE the two ratios, and this is what is taken as the definition for every angle:

$$P=(\cos x,\ \sin x),\qquad \tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}.$$

Rotating past $90^{\circ}$ changes nothing except the **signs of the two coordinates**:
- $0^{\circ}$ to $90^{\circ}$: both coordinates positive, so all three ratios are positive.
- $90^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$: horizontal negative, vertical positive, so only $\sin x$ is positive.
- $180^{\circ}$ to $270^{\circ}$: both negative, so $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are negative but their quotient $\tan x$ is positive.
- $270^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$: horizontal positive, vertical negative, so only $\cos x$ is positive.

That list is [[blue:the CAST diagram]] of the next block, and nothing more.

The symmetry rules come from the same picture. Reflecting $P$ in the vertical axis sends the angle $x$ to $180^{\circ}-x$ and reverses the horizontal coordinate only, so $\sin(180^{\circ}-x)=\sin x$ and $\cos(180^{\circ}-x)=-\cos x$. Reflecting in the horizontal axis sends $x$ to $360^{\circ}-x$ and reverses the vertical coordinate only, so $\cos(360^{\circ}-x)=\cos x$ and $\sin(360^{\circ}-x)=-\sin x$. The same picture explains the asymptotes of $y=\tan x$: at $x=90^{\circ}$ and $x=270^{\circ}$ the horizontal coordinate is $0$, so $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ would divide by zero and is undefined.

assets.caption: A point $P$ at angle $x$ on a circle of radius $1$: its coordinates are $(\cos x,\ \sin x)$. The sign pairs show whether each coordinate is positive or negative in each quadrant, which is where CAST comes from.
assets.purpose: Give the definition of sine and cosine for angles beyond 90 degrees, so that the CAST signs and the 180 - x symmetry rule are consequences a student can see rather than rules to memorise.

theory_blocks.title: The graph of $y=\sin x$
theory_blocks.body: $y=\sin x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$: starts at $(0^{\circ},0)$, rises to a maximum of $1$ at $x=90^{\circ}$, falls back through $0$ at $x=180^{\circ}$, continues to a minimum of $-1$ at $x=270^{\circ}$, and returns to $0$ at $x=360^{\circ}$. It is a smooth wave, symmetric about $x=90^{\circ}$ and about $x=270^{\circ}$, with **period $360^{\circ}$** and **amplitude $1$** (oscillating between $-1$ and $1$).

assets.caption: The graph of $y=\sin x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$: period $360^{\circ}$, amplitude $1$.
assets.purpose: Give a concrete picture of the sine wave's shape, maximum/minimum and period before it is used to count solutions.

theory_blocks.title: The graph of $y=\cos x$
theory_blocks.body: $y=\cos x$ has the same wave shape as sine, but starts at its MAXIMUM: $\cos0^{\circ}=1$, falls through $0$ at $x=90^{\circ}$, reaches a minimum of $-1$ at $x=180^{\circ}$, rises back through $0$ at $x=270^{\circ}$, and returns to $1$ at $x=360^{\circ}$. Same period ($360^{\circ}$) and amplitude ($1$) as sine — it is simply the sine graph shifted $90^{\circ}$ to the left.

assets.caption: The graph of $y=\cos x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$: it starts at its maximum $1$, crosses zero at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$, has its minimum $-1$ at $180^{\circ}$, and returns to $1$ at $360^{\circ}$. Period $360^{\circ}$, amplitude $1$.
assets.purpose: E6.4 requires students to recognise and sketch y = cos x; the block described the curve only in words.

theory_blocks.title: The graph of $y=\tan x$
theory_blocks.body: $y=\tan x$ looks very different: it starts at $0$, rises steeply towards $+\infty$ as $x\to90^{\circ}$ (a **vertical asymptote**, since $\tan90^{\circ}$ is undefined), jumps to $-\infty$ just past $90^{\circ}$ and rises again to $0$ at $x=180^{\circ}$, then repeats the same shape again up to $x=360^{\circ}$ with a second asymptote at $x=270^{\circ}$. Tangent has **period $180^{\circ}$** (half that of sine/cosine) and NO amplitude limit — it is unbounded, taking every real value.

assets.caption: The graph of $y=\tan x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$. The dashed red lines at $x=90^{\circ}$ and $x=270^{\circ}$ are vertical asymptotes, where $\tan x$ is undefined. The same branch shape repeats every $180^{\circ}$, so the period is $180^{\circ}$ and the curve is unbounded.
assets.purpose: E6.4 requires students to recognise and sketch y = tan x; the asymptotes and the three separate branches are very hard to picture from a written description.

theory_blocks.title: Reading the graphs correctly
theory_blocks.body:
- Confusing the period of tangent ($180^{\circ}$) with the period of sine/cosine ($360^{\circ}$).
- Forgetting tangent is undefined (asymptote, not a maximum) at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$.
- Thinking sine/cosine can exceed $1$ or go below $-1$ — [[blue:their amplitude is always exactly $1$]].

theory_blocks.title: The CAST diagram
theory_blocks.body:
The CAST diagram summarises which ratio is positive in each quadrant, read anticlockwise starting from the bottom-right (which gives its name):
- Quadrant 4 ($270^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$): **C**osine positive.
- Quadrant 1 ($0^{\circ}$-$90^{\circ}$): **A**ll positive.
- Quadrant 2 ($90^{\circ}$-$180^{\circ}$): **S**ine positive.
- Quadrant 3 ($180^{\circ}$-$270^{\circ}$): **T**angent positive.
In every quadrant, exactly the one named ratio (or all three, in quadrant 1) is positive; the other two are negative.

assets.caption: CAST diagram: which ratio is positive in each quadrant. Angles are measured anticlockwise from $0^{\circ}$ on the positive $x$-axis, so the quadrant boundaries are at $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$.
assets.purpose: Give a compact visual tool for determining sign and for generating a second solution in each quadrant.

theory_blocks.title: Finding the second solution
theory_blocks.body:
Let $x_1$ be the calculator's (principal) solution.
- $\sin x=k$ ($k>0$): second solution $x_2=180^{\circ}-x_1$ (sine is also positive in quadrant 2).
- $\cos x=k$ ($k>0$): second solution $x_2=360^{\circ}-x_1$ (cosine is also positive in quadrant 4).
- $\tan x=k$: second solution $x_2=x_1+180^{\circ}$ (tangent repeats every $180^{\circ}$).
When $k<0$, the calculator's value $x_0$ for $\sin^{-1}$ or $\tan^{-1}$ is itself negative. For sine, the two solutions are $180^{\circ}-x_0$ (quadrant 3) and $360^{\circ}+x_0$ (quadrant 4); for example $x_0=-17.5^{\circ}$ gives $197.5^{\circ}$ and $342.5^{\circ}$. For tangent, add $180^{\circ}$ and then $360^{\circ}$ to $x_0$. For cosine, $\cos^{-1}$ already gives an angle between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$, so use $360^{\circ}-x_1$ as usual.

assets.caption: Solving $\sin x=k$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$ with $k>0$: the horizontal line $y=k$ cuts the sine curve twice. The calculator gives $x_1$; the second solution is the mirror image of $x_1$ in the line $x=90^{\circ}$, which is $180^{\circ}-x_1$.
assets.purpose: Show why sin x = k has exactly two solutions in the range and why the second one is 180 - x1, instead of asking students to take the rule on trust.

theory_blocks.title: A four-step strategy for solving trig equations
theory_blocks.body:
1. Rearrange the equation into the form $\sin x=k$, $\cos x=k$ or $\tan x=k$.
2. Use the calculator's inverse function to find $x_1$ (adjusting into range if $k<0$, as above).
3. Apply the matching symmetry rule to find every other solution in the required range.
4. Check EVERY candidate against the stated range and discard anything outside it.

theory_blocks.title: Errors specific to equation-solving
theory_blocks.body:
- Giving only the calculator's one value when the question asks for ALL solutions in a range.
- Using the sine/cosine symmetry rule on a tangent equation (or vice versa).
- Accepting a candidate solution outside the stated range, or missing one still inside it after a further $360^{\circ}$/$180^{\circ}$ repeat.

theory_blocks.title: Modelling a periodic real-world quantity
theory_blocks.body: Many real quantities repeat in a wave pattern: the height of a point on a Ferris wheel, the depth of water in a harbour, or the position of a piston. These can be modelled with an expression like $h=a-b\cos x$ or $h=a+b\sin x$, where $a$ shifts the wave up or down and $b$ controls its amplitude (the size of the swing above/below $a$). Solving 'when does the quantity equal a given value?' is exactly the trig-equation method above, applied to the model.

keywords.definition: The angle after which a trigonometric graph's pattern repeats exactly; $360^{\circ}$ for sine and cosine, $180^{\circ}$ for tangent.
Half the distance between a periodic graph's maximum and minimum value; $1$ for sine and cosine (tangent has no amplitude, being unbounded).
A line a graph approaches but never crosses; the tangent graph has vertical asymptotes at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$, where $\tan x$ is undefined.
A diagram of the four quadrants showing which trigonometric ratio (Cosine, All, Sine, Tangent) is positive in each, used to determine signs and find extra solutions.
The single value returned by a calculator's inverse trigonometric function, which may need adjusting or supplementing to find every solution in a given range.
One of the four $90^{\circ}$ sections of the full $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ range: $0$-$90^{\circ}$, $90$-$180^{\circ}$, $180$-$270^{\circ}$, $270$-$360^{\circ}$.

worked_examples.statement: Using the CAST diagram. State whether $\sin150^{\circ}$, $\cos200^{\circ}$ and $\tan200^{\circ}$ are positive or negative, without using a calculator.
reasoning: $150^{\circ}$ lies between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$: quadrant 2, where only sine is positive.
$200^{\circ}$ lies between $180^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$: quadrant 3, where only tangent is positive.
worked_examples.solution: $\sin150^{\circ}$ is positive. $\cos200^{\circ}$ is negative (quadrant 3, cosine not the positive one there). $\tan200^{\circ}$ is positive (quadrant 3, tangent IS the positive one).
worked_examples.interpretation: The CAST diagram answers a sign question in two steps: locate the quadrant, then read off which single ratio (or all three, in quadrant 1) is positive there.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming all three ratios share the same sign in a given quadrant, rather than checking each one individually against CAST.

worked_examples.statement: Solving a sine equation. Solve $\sin x=0.45$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
unknowns: every value of $x$ in the range
reasoning: $x_1=\sin^{-1}(0.45)=26.74^{\circ}$ (2 d.p.) — the calculator's principal solution, in quadrant 1.
Since $0.45>0$, sine is also positive in quadrant 2: second solution $x_2=180^{\circ}-26.74^{\circ}=153.26^{\circ}$.
Check both lie within $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$: yes, and no further repeat ($x_1+360^{\circ}$, etc.) falls in range.
worked_examples.interpretation: A positive sine value always gives exactly two solutions in $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$, symmetric about $90^{\circ}$.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stopping after finding $x_1=26.7^{\circ}$ and not searching for the second, equally valid solution in quadrant 2.

worked_examples.statement: A negative cosine value. Solve $\cos x=-0.35$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
unknowns: every value of $x$ in the range
reasoning: The calculator's $\cos^{-1}(-0.35)=110.49^{\circ}$ (2 d.p.) is already a valid in-range solution (quadrant 2, where cosine is indeed negative), so this IS $x_1$.
Cosine is also negative in quadrant 3: second solution $x_2=360^{\circ}-110.49^{\circ}=249.51^{\circ}$.
Check: $249.51^{\circ}$ is in quadrant 3 as expected, and both solutions lie in range.
worked_examples.interpretation: Unlike $\sin^{-1}$ of a negative number (which returns a negative angle), $\cos^{-1}$ of a negative number returns a valid in-range angle directly, because cosine's principal range already covers $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the calculator's output for a negative cosine must be adjusted into range, when in fact $\cos^{-1}$ already returns a value between $0^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.

worked_examples.statement: A tangent equation. Solve $\tan x=2.5$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
unknowns: every value of $x$ in the range
reasoning: Tangent repeats every $180^{\circ}$ (not $360^{\circ}$): second solution $x_2=68.20^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=248.20^{\circ}$, in quadrant 3, where tangent is indeed also positive.
A further repeat, $68.20^{\circ}+360^{\circ}=428.20^{\circ}$, is outside the range and is rejected.
worked_examples.interpretation: Tangent's shorter period means its two solutions in $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ are exactly $180^{\circ}$ apart, not symmetric about $90^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$ the way sine/cosine solutions are.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using $360^{\circ}-68.20^{\circ}=291.80^{\circ}$ (the cosine-style rule) instead of correctly adding the tangent period of $180^{\circ}$.

guided_exercises.statement: Solve $\cos x=0.2$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
hints: Find $x_1=\cos^{-1}(0.2)$ first with a calculator.
Cosine is positive in quadrants 1 and 4; the quadrant-4 solution is $360^{\circ}-x_1$.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $x_1=\cos^{-1}(0.2)=78.46^{\circ}$. Second solution $=360^{\circ}-78.46^{\circ}=281.54^{\circ}$. Both lie in range: $x=78.5^{\circ}$ or $281.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
common_errors: Using $180^{\circ}-78.46^{\circ}$ (the sine rule) instead of $360^{\circ}-78.46^{\circ}$ for the second cosine solution.

guided_exercises.statement: Solve $\sin x=-0.3$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
hints: The calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(-0.3)$ as a NEGATIVE angle; this is not yet in range, so what must be done to it first?
Sine is negative in quadrants 3 and 4. Use $180^{\circ}-(\text{calculator value})$ for the quadrant-3 solution and $360^{\circ}+(\text{calculator value})$ for the quadrant-4 solution.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Calculator: $\sin^{-1}(-0.3)=-17.46^{\circ}$ (out of range). Quadrant-4 solution: $360^{\circ}+(-17.46^{\circ})=342.54^{\circ}$. Quadrant-3 solution: $180^{\circ}-(-17.46^{\circ})=197.46^{\circ}$. Both lie in range: $x=197.5^{\circ}$ or $342.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
common_errors: Treating the calculator's negative output as simply 'no solution', instead of adjusting it into the $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ range before applying the symmetry rule.

guided_exercises.statement: The height, $h$ metres, of a seat on a Ferris wheel above the ground after it has rotated through angle $x^{\circ}$ is modelled by $h=6-5\cos x$. (a) Find the least and greatest heights. (b) Find the values of $x$ (for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$) when the height is $9\text{ m}$.
hints: (a) $\cos x$ oscillates between $-1$ and $1$; substitute these two extreme values into the formula.
(b) Set $6-5\cos x=9$, rearrange to isolate $\cos x$, then solve exactly as in the worked examples.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) least $=1\text{ m}$, greatest $=11\text{ m}$. (b) $x=126.9^{\circ}$ or $x=233.1^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) Least height uses $\cos x=1$: $h=6-5=1\text{ m}$. Greatest uses $\cos x=-1$: $h=6-5(-1)=11\text{ m}$. (b) $6-5\cos x=9\Rightarrow-5\cos x=3\Rightarrow\cos x=-0.6$. $x_1=\cos^{-1}(-0.6)=126.87^{\circ}$ (already in range, quadrant 2). Second solution $=360^{\circ}-126.87^{\circ}=233.13^{\circ}$. So $x=126.9^{\circ}$ or $233.1^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
common_errors: In (a), assuming the GREATEST height corresponds to $\cos x=1$ (forgetting the minus sign in front of $5\cos x$ reverses which extreme of cosine gives the maximum height).

exercises.statement: State the period and amplitude of (a) $y=\sin x$; (b) $y=\cos x$; (c) $y=\tan x$.
exercises.answer: (a) period $360^{\circ}$, amplitude $1$ (b) period $360^{\circ}$, amplitude $1$ (c) period $180^{\circ}$, amplitude not defined (unbounded).
exercises.full_solution: Sine and cosine both repeat every $360^{\circ}$ and oscillate between $-1$ and $1$ (amplitude $1$). Tangent repeats every $180^{\circ}$ and has no amplitude since it is unbounded, taking every real value between successive asymptotes.
common_errors: Giving $360^{\circ}$ as the period of tangent, confusing it with sine/cosine.

exercises.statement: State, without a calculator, whether each is positive or negative: (a) $\sin200^{\circ}$; (b) $\cos100^{\circ}$; (c) $\tan300^{\circ}$; (d) $\sin350^{\circ}$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $200^{\circ}$: quadrant 3, only tangent positive, so sine negative. (b) $100^{\circ}$: quadrant 2, only sine positive, so cosine negative. (c) $300^{\circ}$: quadrant 4, only cosine positive, so tangent negative. (d) $350^{\circ}$: quadrant 4, only cosine positive, so sine negative.
common_errors: In (c), assuming quadrant 4 makes every ratio behave the same way, rather than checking specifically that cosine (not tangent) is the positive one there.

exercises.statement: Solve $\sin x=0.6$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Giving only $36.9^{\circ}$ and omitting the second quadrant-2 solution.

exercises.statement: Solve $\cos x=0.85$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Reporting only one solution, the recurring the related idea error of trusting the calculator's single output as complete.

exercises.statement: Solve $\tan x=0.9$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Using $360^{\circ}-41.99^{\circ}$ instead of $+180^{\circ}$, the characteristic tangent/sine-cosine rule mix-up.

exercises.statement: Solve $\sin x=-0.5$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
exercises.full_solution: $\sin^{-1}(-0.5)=-30^{\circ}$ (out of range). Quadrant 4 solution: $360^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=330^{\circ}$. Quadrant 3 solution: $180^{\circ}+30^{\circ}=210^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Stopping at the calculator's negative output $-30^{\circ}$ without converting it into two valid in-range solutions.

exercises.statement: Solve $2\sin x+1=0$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$.
exercises.full_solution: Rearranging: $\sin x=-0.5$, as in the previous exercise: $x=210^{\circ}$ or $330^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Solving $2\sin x+1=0$ incorrectly as $\sin x=0.5$ (losing the sign) rather than correctly isolating $\sin x=-0.5$.

exercises.statement: The depth of water in a harbour, $d$ metres, $t$ hours after midnight is modelled (for one tidal cycle) by $d=4+3\sin(30t)^{\circ}$ for $0\le t\le12$. Find the two values of $t$ in this interval when the depth is exactly $5.5\text{ m}$.
common_errors: Forgetting that $x=30t$ is itself an angle, and that the FOUND value of $x$ must still be divided by $30$ to recover $t$ in hours.

exercises.statement: A point $P$ lies on a circle of radius $1$ centred on the origin, at an angle of $210^{\circ}$ measured anticlockwise from the positive horizontal axis. (a) State the sign of each coordinate of $P$ and hence say which of $\sin210^{\circ}$, $\cos210^{\circ}$ and $\tan210^{\circ}$ is positive. (b) Use the circle to explain why $\sin150^{\circ}=\sin30^{\circ}$.
exercises.answer: (a) Both coordinates are negative, so $\cos210^{\circ}<0$ and $\sin210^{\circ}<0$; only $\tan210^{\circ}$ is positive. (b) The point at $150^{\circ}$ is the reflection of the point at $30^{\circ}$ in the vertical axis, so the two points have the same vertical coordinate: $\sin150^{\circ}=\sin30^{\circ}=\tfrac12$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $210^{\circ}$ is between $180^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$, the third quadrant, where the horizontal coordinate $\cos210^{\circ}$ and the vertical coordinate $\sin210^{\circ}$ are both negative. Since $\tan210^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sin210^{\circ}}{\cos210^{\circ}}$ is a negative divided by a negative, it is positive — which is the T of CAST.

(b) $150^{\circ}=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}$. Reflecting the point at $30^{\circ}$ in the vertical axis reverses only the horizontal coordinate, so the vertical coordinate, which is the sine, is unchanged: $\sin150^{\circ}=\sin30^{\circ}=\tfrac12$ (while $\cos150^{\circ}=-\cos30^{\circ}$).
common_errors: Concluding that $\tan210^{\circ}$ is negative because both coordinates are negative; tangent is their quotient, and a negative divided by a negative is positive.

exercises.statement: The diagram shows the graph of $y=\sin x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$, together with the line $y=0.3$. (a) Use the graph to estimate the two solutions of $\sin x=0.3$ in this interval. (b) Now solve $\sin x=0.3$ with a calculator, giving each answer to 1 d.p., and compare.
exercises.answer: (a) About $17^{\circ}$ and about $163^{\circ}$ (any estimate within about $5^{\circ}$ of these is acceptable). (b) $x=17.5^{\circ}$ or $x=162.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
exercises.full_solution: (a) The line $y=0.3$ cuts the curve twice: once on the rising part just after $x=0^{\circ}$ and once on the falling part just before $x=180^{\circ}$. Reading across to the $x$-axis gives roughly $17^{\circ}$ and roughly $163^{\circ}$. (b) $x_1=\sin^{-1}(0.3)=17.4576^{\circ}=17.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.); the second solution is $180^{\circ}-17.4576^{\circ}=162.5424^{\circ}=162.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.). The graph estimates agree with the calculator values, and the graph also confirms there are exactly two solutions in the interval.
common_errors: Reading only the first intersection and reporting a single solution, when the graph plainly shows the line crossing the curve twice.
Reading the $y$-value $0.3$ as if it were an answer in degrees.

assets.caption: The graph of $y=\sin x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$ with the line $y=0.3$ drawn.
assets.purpose: Let the student read the two solutions of $\sin x=0.3$ straight off the graph before checking them with a calculator.

exercises.statement: (a) Sketch the graph of $y=\cos x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$. Mark on your sketch the coordinates of the points where the curve crosses the $x$-axis, and of the maximum and minimum points. (b) State the values of $x$ in the same interval for which $y=\tan x$ is undefined.
exercises.answer: (a) Crosses the $x$-axis at $(90^{\circ},0)$ and $(270^{\circ},0)$; maximum points at $(0^{\circ},1)$ and $(360^{\circ},1)$; minimum point at $(180^{\circ},-1)$. (b) $x=90^{\circ}$ and $x=270^{\circ}$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) The cosine curve starts at its maximum, $\cos0^{\circ}=1$, so the sketch begins at $(0^{\circ},1)$. It falls through $(90^{\circ},0)$ to the minimum $(180^{\circ},-1)$, rises back through $(270^{\circ},0)$ and ends at the maximum $(360^{\circ},1)$. The curve must be a smooth wave between $y=-1$ and $y=1$ (amplitude $1$, period $360^{\circ}$), not a series of straight lines. (b) $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ is undefined where $\cos x=0$, which on this interval is $x=90^{\circ}$ and $x=270^{\circ}$; the graph of $y=\tan x$ has a vertical asymptote at each of these values.
common_errors: Sketching the cosine curve starting at $(0^{\circ},0)$, which is the sine graph, not the cosine graph.
Calling $x=90^{\circ}$ a maximum of $y=\tan x$ instead of an asymptote where the function is undefined.

exercises.statement: Solve for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$, giving exact answers (no calculator): (a) $2\cos x+1=0$; (b) $\sin x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Rearranging, $2\cos x=-1$, so $\cos x=-\dfrac12$. The exact value $\cos60^{\circ}=\dfrac12$ gives the acute reference angle $60^{\circ}$. Cosine is negative in quadrants 2 and 3, so $x=180^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=120^{\circ}$ and $x=180^{\circ}+60^{\circ}=240^{\circ}$. (b) The exact value $\sin60^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ gives the reference angle $60^{\circ}$. Sine is positive in quadrants 1 and 2, so $x=60^{\circ}$ and $x=180^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=120^{\circ}$.
common_errors: In (a), taking $\cos^{-1}$ of $+\dfrac12$ and giving $60^{\circ}$ and $300^{\circ}$, which solve $\cos x=+\dfrac12$ instead.
Rounding to a decimal when the question asks for exact answers obtainable from the exact values of Lesson 6.4.

exam_questions.statement: Solve $3\sin x-1=0$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$, giving both answers to 1 decimal place. [4]
exam_questions.full_solution: Rearranging: $\sin x=\dfrac13=0.3333$. $x_1=\sin^{-1}(0.3333)=19.47^{\circ}$. Second solution $=180^{\circ}-19.47^{\circ}=160.53^{\circ}$. Both lie in range: $x=19.5^{\circ}$ or $160.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
mark_scheme: M1 for correctly rearranging to $\sin x=\tfrac13$
A1 for $x_1=19.5^{\circ}$ (or equivalent unrounded value seen)
M1 for applying $180^{\circ}-x_1$
A1 for $160.5^{\circ}$; both answers required for full marks.
common_errors: Giving only the first solution $19.5^{\circ}$ and stopping there, losing the final two marks.

exam_questions.statement: Solve $3\sin x=7\cos x$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$, giving both answers to 2 decimal places. [5]
exam_questions.full_solution: Dividing both sides by $\cos x$: $3\tan x=7$, so $\tan x=\dfrac73=2.3\overline{3}$. $x_1=\tan^{-1}(2.3333)=66.80^{\circ}$ (2 d.p.). Second solution (tangent, period $180^{\circ}$): $66.80^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=246.80^{\circ}$.
mark_scheme: M1 for dividing both sides by $\cos x$ to reach $\tan x=\tfrac73$
A1 for the correct ratio $\tfrac73$ (not inverted)
A1 for $66.80^{\circ}$
A1 for correctly adding $180^{\circ}$ to get $246.80^{\circ}$.
common_errors: Dividing the wrong way round, reaching $\tan x=\tfrac37$ instead of $\tfrac73$, which gives the wrong pair of angles entirely.

exam_questions.statement:
A Ferris wheel seat's height above the ground, $h$ metres, after rotating through angle $x^{\circ}$ from the bottom is modelled by $h=6-5\cos x$.
(a) State the least and greatest heights of the seat. [2]
(b) Find the two values of $x$ (for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$) for which the height is $3\text{ m}$. Give your answers correct to 1 decimal place. [4]
exam_questions.answer: (a) least $1\text{ m}$, greatest $11\text{ m}$ (b) $x=53.1^{\circ}$ or $x=306.9^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Least height: $\cos x=1\Rightarrow h=6-5=1\text{ m}$. Greatest height: $\cos x=-1\Rightarrow h=6+5=11\text{ m}$. (b) $6-5\cos x=3\Rightarrow-5\cos x=-3\Rightarrow\cos x=0.6$. $x_1=\cos^{-1}(0.6)=53.13^{\circ}$ (quadrant 1). Cosine is also positive in quadrant 4: second solution $=360^{\circ}-53.13^{\circ}=306.87^{\circ}$. So $x=53.1^{\circ}$ or $306.9^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for least $1\text{ m}$; B1 for greatest $11\text{ m}$
(b) M1 for correctly rearranging to $\cos x=0.6$; A1 for $x_1=53.1^{\circ}$; M1 for applying $360^{\circ}-x_1$; A1 for $306.9^{\circ}$.
common_errors: In (a), attaching the maximum height to $\cos x=1$ instead of correctly identifying that the minus sign in front of $5\cos x$ reverses which extreme of cosine gives the maximum.

challenge_questions.statement: Solve $\sin^2x=0.25$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$. (There are four solutions.)
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\sin^2x=0.25\Rightarrow\sin x=\pm0.5$. For $\sin x=0.5$: $x=30^{\circ}$ or $150^{\circ}$. For $\sin x=-0.5$: $x=210^{\circ}$ or $330^{\circ}$. All four values together give the complete solution set.

challenge_questions.statement: Solve $2\cos^2x-\cos x-1=0$ for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$ by factorising as a quadratic in $\cos x$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Let $c=\cos x$: $2c^2-c-1=0\Rightarrow(2c+1)(c-1)=0\Rightarrow c=-0.5$ or $c=1$. For $\cos x=1$: $x=0^{\circ}$ or $360^{\circ}$ (the extremes of the range). For $\cos x=-0.5$: $x_1=120^{\circ}$, second solution $=360^{\circ}-120^{\circ}=240^{\circ}$. Full set: $x=0^{\circ},120^{\circ},240^{\circ},360^{\circ}$.

challenge_questions.statement: The graph of $y=\sin x$ is translated to give $y=\sin x+2$. State the new maximum, minimum, and whether the graph ever crosses the $x$-axis.
challenge_questions.answer: Maximum $=3$, minimum $=1$; the graph never crosses the $x$-axis.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Adding $2$ shifts the whole wave up by $2$: new maximum $=1+2=3$, new minimum $=-1+2=1$. Since the minimum value ($1$) is still above $0$, the curve never reaches $y=0$ and so never crosses the $x$-axis.

challenge_questions.statement: A piston's position (in cm from a fixed point) is modelled by $p=10\sin x-4\cos x$. By evaluating $p$ at $x=0^{\circ},90^{\circ},180^{\circ},270^{\circ}$, decide between which two of these values $p$ first reaches $0$. Then show that $p=0$ leads to $\tan x=0.4$ and find that value of $x$, correct to 2 decimal places.
challenge_questions.answer: $p(0^{\circ})=-4$ and $p(90^{\circ})=10$, so $p$ first reaches $0$ between $x=0^{\circ}$ and $x=90^{\circ}$; there $x=\tan^{-1}(0.4)=21.80^{\circ}$ (2 d.p.).
challenge_questions.full_solution: $p(0^{\circ})=10(0)-4(1)=-4$. $p(90^{\circ})=10(1)-4(0)=10$. Since $p$ changes from negative to positive between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$, it crosses zero there. Setting $p=0$: $10\sin x=4\cos x\Rightarrow\tan x=0.4\Rightarrow x=\tan^{-1}(0.4)=21.80^{\circ}$, which indeed lies between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$, confirming the estimate.

mcq.stem: What is the period of the graph $y=\tan x$?

options.why_wrong: This is the period of sine and cosine, not tangent; tangent's graph repeats twice as often, every $180^{\circ}$.
The asymptotes at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$ are $180^{\circ}$ apart, so $90^{\circ}$ is neither their spacing nor the period of tangent.

options.text: It has no period; it never repeats.
options.why_wrong: Tangent is unbounded (no amplitude limit) but it IS periodic, repeating its exact shape every $180^{\circ}$.

mcq.explanation: $\tan(x+180^{\circ})=\tan x$ for all $x$; the graph's repeating unit is $180^{\circ}$ wide, half that of sine/cosine.

mcq.stem: Given $\sin x=0.7$ and the calculator's value $x_1=44.4^{\circ}$, what is the full solution set for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$?

options.why_wrong: This treats the calculator's single principal value as the complete solution set, missing the equally valid second solution in quadrant 2.
Adding $180^{\circ}$ is the correct rule for a TANGENT equation, not a sine equation; sine's second solution uses $180^{\circ}-x_1$, not $x_1+180^{\circ}$.
$315.6^{\circ}$ is in quadrant 4, where sine is negative; it cannot be a solution of $\sin x=0.7$, a positive value.

mcq.explanation: Sine is positive in quadrants 1 and 2; the second solution is $180^{\circ}-44.4^{\circ}=135.6^{\circ}$.

mcq.stem: Given $\tan x=2.5$ and the calculator's value $x_1=68.2^{\circ}$, what is the second solution for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$?

options.why_wrong: This applies the cosine-style rule ($360^{\circ}-x_1$) to a tangent equation; tangent's own rule is to add its period, $180^{\circ}$, not to reflect around $360^{\circ}$.
This applies the sine-style rule ($180^{\circ}-x_1$); but tangent is negative in quadrant 2, so this angle cannot satisfy $\tan x=2.5$ (a positive value).

options.text: There is no second solution; $68.2^{\circ}$ is the only one.
options.why_wrong: Tangent has period $180^{\circ}$, so a second in-range solution always exists for any value of $x_1$ below $180^{\circ}$: here, $68.2^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=248.2^{\circ}$.

mcq.explanation: Tangent repeats every $180^{\circ}$: $68.2^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=248.2^{\circ}$, which lies in quadrant 3 where tangent is indeed positive.

mcq.stem: Which of these is true about $\cos200^{\circ}$?

options.text: It is positive, since cosine is usually positive.
options.why_wrong: This guesses a sign without checking the quadrant at all; $200^{\circ}$ is in quadrant 3, where cosine is specifically negative.

options.text: It is negative, since $200^{\circ}$ is in quadrant 3 where only tangent is positive.
It cannot be determined without a calculator.
options.why_wrong: The sign can always be determined directly from the CAST diagram once the quadrant is identified, with no calculation needed.

options.text: It is positive, since $200^{\circ}$ is close to $180^{\circ}$, where cosine is $-1$, so nearby values trend positive.
options.why_wrong: This reasoning is backwards: values near $180^{\circ}$ are near cosine's MINIMUM ($-1$), so cosine stays strongly negative there, not trending towards positive.

mcq.explanation: $200^{\circ}$ lies between $180^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$ (quadrant 3), where CAST shows only tangent is positive, so cosine is negative.

mcq.stem: Solving $\sin x=-0.4$, a student finds the calculator value $\sin^{-1}(-0.4)=-23.6^{\circ}$. What should be done next?

options.text: Report $x=-23.6^{\circ}$ as a valid final solution.
options.why_wrong: A negative angle is outside the stated range $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$ and must be converted into an equivalent in-range angle before being accepted.

options.text: Conclude the equation has no solution, since the calculator gave a negative number.
options.why_wrong: A negative calculator output simply signals that the principal value needs adjusting into range; it does not mean the equation is unsolvable, since sine is negative in two whole quadrants (3 and 4).

options.text: Add $360^{\circ}$ to get the quadrant-4 solution ($336.4^{\circ}$), then use $180^{\circ}-(-23.6^{\circ})=203.6^{\circ}$ for the quadrant-3 solution.
Add $180^{\circ}$ to get $156.4^{\circ}$ as the only solution.
options.why_wrong: Adding $180^{\circ}$ is the tangent rule, not the sine rule, and in any case $156.4^{\circ}$ is in quadrant 2 where sine is positive, so it cannot solve $\sin x=-0.4$.

mcq.explanation: Sine is negative in quadrants 3 and 4; adjusting the calculator's negative value gives $336.4^{\circ}$ (quadrant 4), and $180^{\circ}-(-23.6^{\circ})=203.6^{\circ}$ gives the quadrant-3 solution.

flashcards.front: Period of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$
flashcards.back: $360^{\circ}$, with amplitude $1$ (oscillating between $-1$ and $1$).

flashcards.front: Period of $\tan x$
flashcards.back: $180^{\circ}$, with vertical asymptotes at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$ (unbounded, no amplitude).

flashcards.front: CAST diagram quadrant signs
flashcards.back: Q1 ($0$-$90^{\circ}$): all positive. Q2 ($90$-$180^{\circ}$): sine positive. Q3 ($180$-$270^{\circ}$): tangent positive. Q4 ($270$-$360^{\circ}$): cosine positive.

flashcards.front: Second solution rule for $\sin x=k$ ($k>0$), given $x_1$
Second solution rule for $\cos x=k$ ($k>0$), given $x_1$
Second solution rule for $\tan x=k$, given $x_1$
flashcards.back: $x_2=x_1+180^{\circ}$ (not a reflection rule — tangent's own period).

flashcards.front: True or false: a calculator's inverse trig output is always the complete solution set on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$.
flashcards.back: False. It is only the principal (first) solution; a second solution almost always exists and must be found with the matching symmetry rule.

flashcards.front: Sine/cosine second-solution rule vs. tangent's
flashcards.back: Sine/cosine reflect ($180^{\circ}-x_1$ or $360^{\circ}-x_1$) because their period is $360^{\circ}$; tangent simply adds its own shorter period, $180^{\circ}$.

flashcards.front: What to do if $\sin^{-1}(k)$ or $\tan^{-1}(k)$ gives a negative angle
flashcards.back: Sine: use $180^{\circ}-(\text{calculator value})$ and $360^{\circ}+(\text{calculator value})$. Tangent: add $180^{\circ}$, then $360^{\circ}$, to the calculator value.

flashcards.front: Why does $\cos^{-1}$ of a negative number NOT need adjusting into range, unlike $\sin^{-1}$ or $\tan^{-1}$?
flashcards.back: Cosine's principal value range is already $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$, which fully overlaps the required $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ range, so the calculator's output is always already valid.

flashcards.front: Modelling height with $h=a-b\cos x$ — what do $a$ and $b$ control?
flashcards.back: $a$ is the midline (average height); $b$ is the amplitude (size of the swing above/below the midline).

flashcards.front: How many solutions does $\sin^2x=0.25$ have on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$, and why?
flashcards.back: Four: taking the square root gives TWO equations, $\sin x=0.5$ and $\sin x=-0.5$, each contributing two solutions.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Believing a calculator's inverse trig function (e.g. $\sin^{-1}$) gives the COMPLETE set of solutions to an equation on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The calculator produces a single confident-looking number, and earlier work (Lesson 6.2) only ever needed the one acute angle inside a triangle, so there was never a reason to look for a second solution before.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner gives only one value of $x$ when asked to 'solve... for $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$', even though the graph clearly crosses the target height twice (for sine/cosine) within that range.
misconceptions.correct_model: The calculator's answer is only the FIRST (principal) solution. For $\sin x=k$ ($k>0$) a second solution is $180^{\circ}-x_1$; for $\cos x=k$ a second solution is $360^{\circ}-x_1$; for $\tan x=k$ a second solution is $x_1+180^{\circ}$. Always sketch the graph and count the crossings before declaring the solution set complete.
misconceptions.remediation: Make 'how many solutions does the graph show in this range?' the compulsory first step of every trig-equation question, before writing any answer down.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Guessing the sign of $\sin,\cos$ or $\tan$ for an angle beyond $90^{\circ}$ instead of using the CAST quadrant rule.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Up to Lesson 6.2 every angle used was acute (inside a triangle, between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$), where all three ratios are positive, so there was never a reason to think about sign at all.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states $\cos200^{\circ}$ or $\sin300^{\circ}$ is positive without checking which quadrant the angle lies in.
misconceptions.correct_model: Quadrant 1 ($0^{\circ}$-$90^{\circ}$): all positive. Quadrant 2 ($90^{\circ}$-$180^{\circ}$): only sine positive. Quadrant 3 ($180^{\circ}$-$270^{\circ}$): only tangent positive. Quadrant 4 ($270^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$): only cosine positive (CAST, read anticlockwise from quadrant 4).
misconceptions.remediation: Sketch the CAST diagram and physically locate the angle in its quadrant before stating or using a sign.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Using the sine/cosine second-solution rule ($180^{\circ}-x$ or $360^{\circ}-x$) when solving a tangent equation, instead of adding $180^{\circ}$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The three ratios are often taught together and their second-solution rules are easy to blur into one 'universal' rule, especially since all three graphs are periodic.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For $\tan x=2.5$, $x_1=68.2^{\circ}$, the learner writes $360^{\circ}-68.2^{\circ}=291.8^{\circ}$ as the second solution instead of $68.2^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=248.2^{\circ}$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Tangent has period $180^{\circ}$ (not $360^{\circ}$ like sine/cosine), and is positive in quadrants 1 AND 3. Its second solution is always $x_1+180^{\circ}$, found by adding the period directly rather than reflecting around $180^{\circ}$ or $360^{\circ}$.
misconceptions.remediation: Sketch the tangent graph specifically (not sine/cosine) whenever solving a tangent equation, to see the $180^{\circ}$ repeat directly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Forgetting to check whether a found solution actually lies within the range given in the question (e.g. accepting $x=428.2^{\circ}$ when the range is $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Adding or subtracting $180^{\circ}$/$360^{\circ}$ repeatedly to generate more solutions can be done mechanically without re-checking against the stated range each time.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's final answer list includes a value outside the specified interval, or a value is silently omitted even though a within-range solution should have been generated at some repeat of the period.
misconceptions.correct_model: After generating every candidate solution (using the appropriate symmetry rule, repeated as many times as necessary), check EACH one against the question's stated range and discard any outside it, and confirm none inside the range has been missed.
misconceptions.remediation: Write down the full interval (e.g. '$0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$') next to the working and tick off each candidate solution against it explicitly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting only the calculator's single principal solution when a question on $0^{\circ}$-$360^{\circ}$ asks for all solutions.
common_mistakes.why: The calculator's confident single output feels complete, and earlier triangle-trigonometry work never required a second answer.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always ask 'how many times does the graph cross this height in this range?' before declaring the answer complete.

common_mistakes.mistake: Guessing the sign of a ratio for an angle beyond $90^{\circ}$ instead of using the CAST diagram.
common_mistakes.why: All ratios were positive throughout the acute-angle-only work of Lesson 6.2, so sign was never an issue before.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Sketch the CAST diagram and locate the angle's quadrant before stating any sign.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the sine/cosine second-solution rule on a tangent equation.
common_mistakes.why: The three ratios' rules are easy to blur together since all three graphs are periodic.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Sketch the tangent graph specifically when solving a tangent equation, to see its $180^{\circ}$ repeat directly rather than relying on a memorised (and easily confused) rule.

exam_notes: A trig equation on a stated range (e.g. $0^{\circ}\le x\le360^{\circ}$) almost always has MORE THAN ONE solution; the question's mark scheme usually allocates marks specifically for finding the second (or further) solution, not just the first.
Sketch the relevant graph (sine, cosine or tangent) as a first step in any 'solve for the given range' question; it instantly shows how many solutions to expect and roughly where they are.

Be careful with a calculator's negative output $x_0$ for $\sin^{-1}$ or $\tan^{-1}$: for sine the solutions in range are $180^{\circ}-x_0$ and $360^{\circ}+x_0$; for tangent they are $x_0+180^{\circ}$ and $x_0+360^{\circ}$.

In a modelling question, substitute the two extreme values of $\sin x$ or $\cos x$ ($-1$ and $1$) to find the greatest/least value of the modelled quantity, watching carefully for a minus sign that reverses which extreme gives the maximum.

summary.big_idea: Beyond $90^{\circ}$, $\sin,\cos,\tan$ form smooth repeating graphs (period $360^{\circ}$ for sine/cosine, $180^{\circ}$ for tangent); a calculator's inverse function finds only ONE solution of an equation, and the CAST diagram's quadrant symmetry must be used to find every other solution within a stated range.
key_points: $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$: period $360^{\circ}$, amplitude $1$; $y=\tan x$: period $180^{\circ}$, unbounded, asymptotes at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$.
CAST diagram: Q1 all positive, Q2 sine positive, Q3 tangent positive, Q4 cosine positive.
Second-solution rules from the calculator's value $x_1$: sine $\to180^{\circ}-x_1$; cosine $\to360^{\circ}-x_1$; tangent $\to x_1+180^{\circ}$.

A negative $\sin^{-1}$ output $x_0$ gives the solutions $180^{\circ}-x_0$ and $360^{\circ}+x_0$; a negative $\tan^{-1}$ output gives $x_0+180^{\circ}$ and $x_0+360^{\circ}$; $\cos^{-1}$ of a negative number is already in range.
Always check every candidate solution against the question's stated range before finalising the answer.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A calculator's inverse trig output is only the FIRST solution: sketch the graph (or use CAST), apply the matching symmetry rule (sine: $180^{\circ}-x_1$; cosine: $360^{\circ}-x_1$; tangent: $x_1+180^{\circ}$) to find every other solution, and check each one lies within the stated range.

epistemic_overrides.note: A four-step strategy for solving trig equations

06_Non-Right-Angled_Triangles_The_Sine_a.title: Non-Right-Angled Triangles: The Sine and Cosine Rules
06_Non-Right-Angled_Triangles_The_Sine_a.subject: Mathematics
06_Non-Right-Angled_Triangles_The_Sine_a.course_label: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 · Trigonometry · Extended only

objectives.statement: Use the sine rule to find an unknown side or angle in a non-right-angled triangle.
Use the cosine rule to find an unknown side (given two sides and the included angle) or an unknown angle (given three sides).
Recognise the ambiguous case of the sine rule and decide whether one or two triangles satisfy the given information.
Find the area of any triangle using Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$, and select the correct rule (sine, cosine or area) for a given triangle problem.

prerequisites.statement: Use SOH-CAH-TOA to find a side or angle in a RIGHT-angled triangle (from Lesson 6.2).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The sine and cosine rules are needed precisely because SOH-CAH-TOA only works when there is a right angle; recognising that absence is the trigger for using these new rules.

prerequisites.statement: Use the angle sum of a triangle ($180^{\circ}$) to find a missing angle.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The sine rule is frequently combined with the angle sum to find a third angle once two are known, and the ambiguous case specifically requires checking that a candidate angle still leaves $180^{\circ}$ available for the remaining two angles.

prerequisites.statement: Rearrange a simple equation to isolate an unknown, including one appearing inside a trigonometric function (e.g. solving $\sin B=0.47$ for $B$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every sine/cosine rule calculation ends with an equation of exactly this shape that must be rearranged and then solved with an inverse trigonometric function.

prerequisites.statement: Substitute values into a formula and evaluate it correctly, respecting order of operations (from Lesson 6.1, Pythagoras).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The cosine rule and area formula are substitution-heavy; a single misplaced term or order-of-operations slip gives a completely wrong triangle.

diagnostic_items.question: Triangle $ABC$ has no right angle, with angle $A=50^{\circ}$, $AB=10\text{ cm}$ and you need to find $BC$. Can SOH-CAH-TOA be used directly?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. SOH-CAH-TOA only applies in a right-angled triangle; since no angle here is $90^{\circ}$, the sine or cosine rule must be used instead.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, just label one side 'opposite' and one 'adjacent' as usual.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Applies the right-angled-triangle ratios regardless of whether a right angle is actually present, not recognising that SOH-CAH-TOA is only valid when one angle is exactly $90^{\circ}$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests the single most important trigger for this whole lesson: recognising the ABSENCE of a right angle as the signal to switch from SOH-CAH-TOA to the sine/cosine rule.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Before starting any triangle problem, explicitly check for a right-angle marker; if none exists, name it as a 'general triangle' requiring the sine or cosine rule.

diagnostic_items.question: In a triangle, two angles are $50^{\circ}$ and $110^{\circ}$. What is the third angle?

common_wrong_answers.answer: $360^{\circ}-50^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=200^{\circ}$, confusing the triangle angle sum with the quadrilateral angle sum.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Uses the wrong total angle sum (360 degrees, for a quadrilateral) instead of the correct 180 degrees for a triangle.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Confirms the basic angle-sum fact is secure before it is combined with sine-rule calculations, especially for the ambiguous case where this check is essential.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch any triangle and physically label all three angles, summing them to confirm $180^{\circ}$ before moving to sine-rule work.

diagnostic_items.question: If $\sin B=0.6$, is $B=36.87^{\circ}$ the only possible value of $B$ in a triangle?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No — sine is also positive for the obtuse angle $180^{\circ}-36.87^{\circ}=143.13^{\circ}$, which is also a valid triangle angle.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, since a calculator only gives one answer.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Does not recognise that a triangle angle can be obtuse, and that sine is positive for both an acute angle and its supplementary obtuse angle.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This is the exact root of the sine-rule's ambiguous case: whether the learner knows BOTH an acute angle and its supplement can have the same positive sine value.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revisit Lesson 6.5's CAST diagram: sine is positive in quadrants 1 and 2, i.e. for both an acute angle and its $180^{\circ}$-supplement.

diagnostic_items.question: Evaluate $7^2+9^2-2\times7\times9\times\cos55^{\circ}$ using the correct order of operations.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Subtracting $2\times7\times9$ and $\cos55^{\circ}$ as two separate steps in the wrong order, or squaring the entire subtraction expression instead of just $7$ and $9$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Mishandles the order of operations in the cosine rule's right-hand side, a frequent source of arithmetic error even when the correct formula has been written down.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Confirms the learner can correctly evaluate the cosine rule's right-hand side numerically before it is used to find an actual triangle side.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Break the substitution into clearly separated written steps: compute the two squares, then the product $2\times7\times9$, then multiply by $\cos55^{\circ}$, then combine.

theory_blocks.title: When SOH-CAH-TOA is not enough
theory_blocks.body: SOH-CAH-TOA needs a right angle to define 'opposite' and 'adjacent' meaningfully. Most real triangles — a triangular field, a surveying problem, a slice of a polygon — have no right angle at all. Two new rules extend trigonometry to ANY triangle: [[blue:the sine rule]] (for pairs of a side and its opposite angle) and [[orange:the cosine rule]] (for three sides and the angle between two of them).

theory_blocks.title: The sine rule
theory_blocks.body:
In any triangle $ABC$, with side $a$ opposite angle $A$, side $b$ opposite angle $B$, and side $c$ opposite angle $C$:
$$\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}.$$
Use the version with the unknown on top ($\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}$) to find a SIDE, given one full pair (a side and its opposite angle) plus one more angle or side. Use it upside down ($\dfrac{\sin A}{a}=\dfrac{\sin B}{b}$) to find an ANGLE.

assets.caption: Standard labelling: side $a$ (lower-case) is opposite vertex/angle $A$ (upper-case), and so on.
assets.purpose: Fix the side/angle labelling convention used consistently throughout the sine and cosine rule.

theory_blocks.title: Which rule, which way up
theory_blocks.body: The sine rule needs a complete OPPOSITE PAIR (one side and the angle directly across the triangle from it) to be known, plus one more piece of information (another side or angle). [[red:If no complete opposite pair is known]] — for example, two sides and the angle BETWEEN them — the sine rule cannot be started, and [[green:the cosine rule must be used instead]].

theory_blocks.title: The cosine rule
theory_blocks.body:
To find a side, given two sides and the INCLUDED angle:
$$a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A.$$
To find an angle, given all three sides (rearranged):
$$\cos A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}.$$
Here $A$ is always the angle opposite side $a$, and (in the side-finding version) the angle INCLUDED between the two known sides $b$ and $c$.

theory_blocks.title: Three setup errors with the cosine rule
theory_blocks.body:
- Using the cosine rule's side-finding version when the known angle is NOT between the two known sides (the sine rule is needed instead).
- Getting the order of operations wrong when substituting: square $b$ and $c$ FIRST, then subtract the whole term $2bc\cos A$.
- When finding an angle from three sides, forgetting that $\cos A$ can come out NEGATIVE (meaning $A$ is obtuse) — this is a normal, valid result, not a sign of an error.

theory_blocks.title: The ambiguous case
theory_blocks.body:
When the sine rule is used to find an angle (given two sides and a non-included angle), sine's positive value in both quadrant 1 and quadrant 2 means there can be TWO valid triangles. If $\sin B=k$ gives an acute angle $B_1$, the obtuse supplement $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$ is ALSO a valid triangle angle exactly when $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$ (there is still room left for the third angle). If $A+B_2\ge180^{\circ}$, only $B_1$ is valid — the obtuse triangle would leave no room for the third angle.
When the known angle $A$ is acute, this happens exactly when the side opposite it ($a$) satisfies $b\sin A<a<b$: the known side is long enough to reach the base line in two different places, but shorter than $b$.

assets.caption: The ambiguous case with $A=36^{\circ}$, $b=11$ and $a=7$: an arc of radius $a$ centred at $C$ cuts the base line at $B_1$ and $B_2$, so two triangles fit the same data — one with $B=112.5^{\circ}$ and one with $B=67.5^{\circ}$. Two triangles exist because $b\sin A=6.47<a=7<b=11$.
assets.purpose: Show why the sine rule can give two valid angles: the arc of radius $a$ meets the base line twice.
