theory_blocks.title: A three-step check for the ambiguous case
theory_blocks.body:
1. Find the acute angle $B_1=\sin^{-1}(k)$ as usual.
2. Compute the obtuse supplement $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$.
3. Check: is $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$? If yes, BOTH $B_1$ and $B_2$ give valid triangles (state both, and the two different third angles and remaining sides that follow). If no, only $B_1$ is valid.

theory_blocks.title: The area of any triangle
theory_blocks.body:
When two sides and the INCLUDED angle are known, the area of a triangle is:
$$\text{Area}=\frac12ab\sin C,$$
where $C$ is the angle between sides $a$ and $b$. This generalises the familiar $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$ formula: $b\sin C$ IS the height of the triangle when $a$ is taken as the base.
When only the three sides are known, find one angle first with the cosine rule, then apply this formula.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing the right rule
theory_blocks.body:
- Right angle present? Use SOH-CAH-TOA (and ordinary Pythagoras), not these new rules.
- A complete opposite side/angle pair known, plus one more piece? Sine rule.
- Two sides and the INCLUDED angle known, want the third side (or the area)? Cosine rule for the side / Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$.
- All three sides known, want an angle? Cosine rule, rearranged.
- Two sides and a NON-included angle known, want the third side or an angle? Sine rule (and check for the ambiguous case if finding an angle).

theory_blocks.title: Bearings problems with the sine/cosine rule
theory_blocks.body: A bearings problem with two legs that are NOT at right angles to each other needs the interior angle at the 'turn' point, found from the two bearings (the angle between the incoming and outgoing direction), before the sine or cosine rule can be applied to the resulting non-right-angled triangle.

keywords.definition: The relationship $\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}=\dfrac{c}{\sin C}$, valid in any triangle, used when a complete side/opposite-angle pair is known.
The relationship $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$ (or its rearrangement for an angle), valid in any triangle, used with two sides and the included angle or all three sides.
The angle positioned directly between two specific named sides of a triangle.
A sine-rule situation where two sides and a non-included angle produce TWO valid triangles, one with an acute and one with an obtuse version of the unknown angle.
Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$, where $C$ is the angle included between sides $a$ and $b$.
A side and the angle directly across the triangle from it, labelled with the same letter in lower/upper case (e.g. side $a$ and angle $A$).

worked_examples.statement: Finding a side with the sine rule. In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=71^{\circ}$, angle $B=42^{\circ}$ and $a=9.4\text{ cm}$. Find $b$.
reasoning: A complete opposite pair ($a,A$) is known, plus the angle $B$ opposite the required side: sine rule applies.
$\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}\Rightarrow b=\dfrac{a\sin B}{\sin A}$.
Substitute and evaluate.
worked_examples.interpretation: Finding a side with the sine rule is a direct substitution once a complete opposite pair and the angle opposite the target side are identified.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Inverting the fraction, writing $b=\dfrac{a\sin A}{\sin B}$ instead of correctly matching each side with its OWN opposite angle on each side of the equation.

worked_examples.statement: Finding a side with the cosine rule. In triangle $ABC$, $b=7\text{ cm}$, $c=9\text{ cm}$ and the included angle $A=55^{\circ}$. Find $a$.
reasoning: Two sides and their included angle are known, and the OPPOSITE side is wanted: cosine rule, side-finding version.
$a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A=7^2+9^2-2\times7\times9\times\cos55^{\circ}$.
Evaluate step by step: squares first, then the product term, then combine, then square root.
worked_examples.interpretation: The cosine rule generalises Pythagoras: when $A=90^{\circ}$, $\cos A=0$ and the formula collapses exactly to $a^2=b^2+c^2$.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting the final square root, giving the answer as $57.7\text{ cm}$ (the value of $a^2$) instead of $a=7.60\text{ cm}$.

worked_examples.statement: Finding the largest angle. A triangle has sides $5\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$. Find its largest angle.
reasoning: The largest angle is always opposite the LONGEST side: here, opposite the side of length $10$.
Label the side of length $10$ as $c$ (so the angle sought is $C$), and use the rearranged cosine rule.
$\cos C=\dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}=\dfrac{5^2+7^2-10^2}{2\times5\times7}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A negative value of $\cos C$ is expected and meaningful here: it correctly signals that the largest angle in this particular triangle is obtuse.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating the negative value of $\cos C$ as evidence of an arithmetic error and 'correcting' it to positive, instead of recognising it correctly indicates an obtuse angle.

worked_examples.statement: Area of a triangle. In triangle $ABC$, $a=8\text{ cm}$, $b=11\text{ cm}$, and the included angle $C=38^{\circ}$. Find the area.
reasoning: Two sides and the angle BETWEEN them are known: Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$ applies directly.
Substitute the three values and evaluate.
worked_examples.solution: Area $=\tfrac12\times8\times11\times\sin38^{\circ}=44\times0.6157=27.09\text{ cm}^2$ (4 s.f., i.e. $27.1\text{ cm}^2$ to 3 s.f.).
worked_examples.interpretation: The area formula needs exactly the same 'two sides and the included angle' configuration as the cosine rule's side-finding version.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using an angle from the triangle that is NOT between the two substituted sides $a$ and $b$, giving a meaningless area value.

worked_examples.statement: The ambiguous case. In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=36^{\circ}$, $a=7\text{ cm}$ and $b=11\text{ cm}$. Find the possible value(s) of angle $B$.
reasoning: A complete pair ($a,A$) plus a second side ($b$) is known, with the angle sought ($B$) opposite that second side: sine rule for an angle.
$\dfrac{\sin B}{b}=\dfrac{\sin A}{a}\Rightarrow\sin B=\dfrac{b\sin A}{a}=\dfrac{11\sin36^{\circ}}{7}$.

Check the ambiguous-case condition: $B_1=\sin^{-1}(0.9237)=67.47^{\circ}$; $B_2=180^{\circ}-67.47^{\circ}=112.53^{\circ}$. Since $A+B_2=36^{\circ}+112.53^{\circ}=148.53^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$, both are valid.
worked_examples.solution: $B=67.5^{\circ}$ or $B=112.5^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.) — TWO valid triangles exist.
worked_examples.interpretation: Because $b>a$ here (the side opposite the UNKNOWN angle is longer than the side opposite the KNOWN angle), a genuine ambiguous case can arise; both solutions must be checked against the angle-sum condition before being accepted.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reporting only $B=67.5^{\circ}$, the calculator's direct output, without checking whether the obtuse supplement also gives a valid triangle.

guided_exercises.statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=48^{\circ}$, angle $B=67^{\circ}$ and $a=10.2\text{ cm}$. Find $b$.
hints: Identify the complete opposite pair ($a,A$) and the angle ($B$) opposite the side you need.
Use $b=\dfrac{a\sin B}{\sin A}$, substituting carefully.
common_errors: Dividing by $\sin B$ instead of $\sin A$, inverting the correct form of the sine rule.

guided_exercises.statement: In triangle $ABC$, $b=10\text{ cm}$, $c=14\text{ cm}$ and the included angle $A=72^{\circ}$. Find $a$.
hints: Confirm $A$ is the angle INCLUDED between the two given sides $b$ and $c$.
$a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$ — substitute and evaluate the right-hand side fully before taking the square root.
common_errors: Omitting the final square root and giving $209\text{ cm}$ (the value of $a^2$) as the answer.

guided_exercises.statement: A triangle has sides $11\text{ cm}$, $13\text{ cm}$ and $19\text{ cm}$. Find the angle opposite the longest side.
hints: The angle opposite the longest side ($19$) is the LARGEST angle in the triangle — label it $C$.
Use $\cos C=\dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$ with $a=11,b=13,c=19$.
common_errors: Labelling the wrong side as $c$ (not the longest), which finds a different, smaller angle instead of the one actually requested.

exercises.statement: For each triangle described, state whether you would use the sine rule or the cosine rule: (a) two angles and one side known; (b) two sides and the included angle known, want the third side; (c) three sides known, want an angle; (d) two sides and a non-included angle known, want the third side.
exercises.answer: (a) sine rule (b) cosine rule (c) cosine rule (d) sine rule.
exercises.full_solution: (a) A complete opposite pair can always be formed when two angles and a side are known (find the third angle first if needed): sine rule. (b) Two sides and their INCLUDED angle, want the third side: cosine rule. (c) All three sides, want an angle: cosine rule (rearranged). (d) Two sides and a non-included angle: no two-side-one-included-angle configuration exists, so sine rule.
common_errors: In (d), reaching for the cosine rule since 'two sides are known', without checking that the known angle is NOT the included one.

exercises.statement: In triangle $PQR$, angle $P=55^{\circ}$, angle $Q=65^{\circ}$ and $p=8\text{ cm}$. Find $q$.
exercises.full_solution: $q=\dfrac{p\sin Q}{\sin P}=\dfrac{8\times\sin65^{\circ}}{\sin55^{\circ}}=\dfrac{8\times0.9063}{0.8192}=8.85\text{ cm}$.
common_errors: Matching $p$ with $\sin P$ incorrectly on the wrong side of the equation.

exercises.statement: In triangle $XYZ$, angle $X=80^{\circ}$, $x=15\text{ cm}$ and $y=9\text{ cm}$. Find angle $Y$ (there is only one valid solution here — explain briefly why).
exercises.answer: $Y=36.2^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.); only one solution because $x>y$ so angle $Y$ must be smaller than angle $X$, ruling out an obtuse $Y$.
exercises.full_solution: $\sin Y=\dfrac{y\sin X}{x}=\dfrac{9\times\sin80^{\circ}}{15}=\dfrac{9\times0.9848}{15}=0.5909$. $Y_1=\sin^{-1}(0.5909)=36.22^{\circ}$. Checking the obtuse supplement $Y_2=143.78^{\circ}$: $X+Y_2=80^{\circ}+143.78^{\circ}=223.78^{\circ}>180^{\circ}$, impossible, so only $Y=36.2^{\circ}$ is valid.
common_errors: Not checking the obtuse supplement at all, or checking it but failing to correctly reject it based on the angle-sum condition.

exercises.statement: In triangle $ABC$, $a=6\text{ cm}$, $b=8\text{ cm}$ and the included angle $C=50^{\circ}$. Find $c$.
common_errors: Using the wrong letter's formula, e.g. $a^2=\ldots$ instead of $c^2=\ldots$, when $C$ is the included angle between $a$ and $b$.

exercises.statement: A triangle has sides $8\text{ cm}, 10\text{ cm}, 13\text{ cm}$. Find its smallest angle.
exercises.full_solution: The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side, $8$. Label it $A$: $\cos A=\dfrac{10^2+13^2-8^2}{2\times10\times13}=\dfrac{100+169-64}{260}=\dfrac{205}{260}=0.7885$. $A=\cos^{-1}(0.7885)=37.96^{\circ}\approx38.0^{\circ}$ (1 d.p.).
common_errors: Finding the angle opposite a different side by mislabelling, giving a larger angle than the genuinely smallest one.

exercises.statement: In triangle $ABC$, $a=9\text{ cm}$, $b=12\text{ cm}$ and the included angle $C=65^{\circ}$. Find the area.
exercises.full_solution: Area $=\tfrac12\times9\times12\times\sin65^{\circ}=54\times0.9063=48.94\text{ cm}^2$.
common_errors: Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ and giving $9\times12\times\sin65^{\circ}=97.9\text{ cm}^2$, double the true area.

exercises.statement: A triangle has sides $11\text{ cm}, 13\text{ cm}, 19\text{ cm}$ (the same triangle as the guided exercise). Find its area.
exercises.full_solution: Using the angle $C=104.37^{\circ}$ found in the guided exercise (opposite the side $19$, included between the sides $11$ and $13$): Area $=\tfrac12\times11\times13\times\sin104.37^{\circ}=71.5\times0.9684=69.26\text{ cm}^2$.
common_errors: Using the side of length $19$ as one of the two sides in the area formula, instead of the two shorter sides that actually enclose the angle $C$ just found.

exercises.statement: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=50^{\circ}$, $a=5\text{ cm}$ and $b=11\text{ cm}$. Show that this situation gives NO valid triangle, and explain why.
exercises.answer: No valid triangle: $\sin B=\dfrac{11\sin50^{\circ}}5=1.685$, which is impossible since sine can never exceed $1$.
exercises.full_solution: $\sin B=\dfrac{b\sin A}{a}=\dfrac{11\times\sin50^{\circ}}{5}=\dfrac{11\times0.766}{5}=1.685$. Since $\sin B$ can never be greater than $1$, no angle $B$ exists that fits these values — geometrically, side $a=5\text{ cm}$ is too short to reach from $C$ down to the line through $A$ at the given angle, so no triangle with these measurements can be drawn at all.
common_errors: Not noticing the computed value of $\sin B$ exceeds $1$, and attempting to force a calculator inverse-sine calculation on it regardless (which would produce a math error, masking the real issue that no triangle exists).

exercises.statement: A ship sails from port $A$ to port $B$, a distance of $40\text{ km}$ on a bearing of $070^{\circ}$, then from $B$ to port $C$, a distance of $25\text{ km}$ on a bearing of $150^{\circ}$. Find the distance $AC$.
exercises.full_solution: The interior angle at $B$ (between $BA$ reversed and $BC$) is found from the bearings: the bearing back from $B$ to $A$ is $070^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=250^{\circ}$, and the bearing from $B$ to $C$ is $150^{\circ}$, so angle $ABC=250^{\circ}-150^{\circ}=100^{\circ}$. Cosine rule: $AC^2=40^2+25^2-2\times40\times25\times\cos100^{\circ}=1600+625-2000\times(-0.1736)=2225+347.3=2572.3$. $AC=\sqrt{2572.3}=50.7\text{ km}$ (3 s.f.).
common_errors: Using the DIFFERENCE between the two given bearings ($150^{\circ}-070^{\circ}=80^{\circ}$) directly as the interior triangle angle, instead of correctly accounting for the reversed bearing back from $B$ to $A$.

exercises.statement: In triangle $ABC$, $a=8\text{ cm}$, $c=11\text{ cm}$, angle $A=42.3^{\circ}$ and angle $B=70^{\circ}$. A student wants the area and writes Area $=\tfrac12\times8\times11\times\sin42.3^{\circ}$. Explain why this is WRONG, and find the area correctly.
exercises.answer: Wrong because $42.3^{\circ}$ (angle $A$) is not the angle included between sides $a$ and $c$; correct area $=41.3\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.), found using angle $B$, which IS the included angle.
exercises.full_solution: Angle $A=42.3^{\circ}$ is opposite side $a$, so it is NOT between sides $a$ and $c$ (angle $B$, between $a$ and $c$, is the one needed, and it is already given as $70^{\circ}$). Correct area $=\tfrac12\times a\times c\times\sin B=\tfrac12\times8\times11\times\sin70^{\circ}=44\times0.9397=41.3\text{ cm}^2$.
common_errors: Substituting whichever angle is given first/most prominently into the area formula without checking it is genuinely the included angle for the two sides being used — the the related idea error.

exam_questions.statement:
A triangular field has sides $9\text{ m}$, $12\text{ m}$ and $17\text{ m}$.
(a) Find the angle opposite the longest side. [3]
(b) Find the area of the field. [3]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correctly rearranged cosine rule with the longest side labelled $c$; A1 for $\cos C=\dfrac{-64}{216}=-0.2963$ (negative, correctly signalling an obtuse angle); A1 for $107.2^{\circ}$

(b) M1 for Area $=\tfrac12\times9\times12\times\sin C$ using the angle found in (a) and the two sides that include it; A1 for correct substitution; A1 for $51.6\text{ m}^2$ (follow-through from (a) allowed).
common_errors: In (a), treating the negative cosine value as an error and reporting the acute supplement $72.8^{\circ}$ instead of the correct obtuse angle.

exam_questions.statement:
In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=36^{\circ}$, $a=7\text{ cm}$ and $b=11\text{ cm}$.
(a) Find the two possible values of angle $B$, showing that both are valid. [4]
(b) For the triangle in which $B$ is OBTUSE, find angle $C$. [1]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for $\sin B=\tfrac{11\sin36^{\circ}}7$; A1 for $B_1=67.47^{\circ}$; M1 for finding $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$; A1 for correctly checking $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$ and stating both values
(b) B1 for $31.47^{\circ}$ (follow-through from the obtuse $B$ in (a)).
common_errors: Reporting only $B=67.47^{\circ}$ in (a), omitting the valid second solution entirely, which also forfeits any chance of answering (b) correctly.

exam_questions.statement: Two ships leave port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ sails on a bearing of $062^{\circ}$ for $14\text{ km}$ to point $A$. Ship $B$ sails on a bearing of $150^{\circ}$ for $10\text{ km}$ to point $B$. Find the distance $AB$ between the two ships.
exam_questions.full_solution: The angle $APB$ between the two bearings is $150^{\circ}-062^{\circ}=88^{\circ}$. Cosine rule: $AB^2=14^2+10^2-2\times14\times10\times\cos88^{\circ}=196+100-280\times0.0349=296-9.77=286.23$. $AB=\sqrt{286.23}=16.92\ldots$, so $AB=16.9\text{ km}$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for correctly finding the included angle at $P$ as the difference of the two bearings ($88^{\circ}$)
M1 for the cosine rule correctly set up with $14,10,88^{\circ}$
A1 for $AB^2=286.2$ (or equivalent unrounded value)
A1 for $AB=16.9\text{ km}$.
common_errors: Adding the two bearings instead of subtracting them to find the angle at $P$, since both bearings are measured from the same reference north direction at the same point.

challenge_questions.statement: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ has $AB=8\text{ cm}$, $BC=10\text{ cm}$, angle $ABC=100^{\circ}$, $CD=7\text{ cm}$, $DA=9\text{ cm}$. Find the length of diagonal $AC$, and hence find angle $ADC$.

A regular pentagon has side length $6\text{ cm}$. By splitting it into 5 congruent isosceles triangles meeting at the centre (each with apex angle $72^{\circ}$) and using the area formula, find the area of the pentagon, correct to 3 s.f.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Each isosceles triangle has two equal sides $r$ (the distance from centre to vertex) with included angle $72^{\circ}$ and base $6$. Using the sine rule in half of one triangle, or directly: each triangle's area can instead be found via $\tfrac12r^2\sin72^{\circ}$ once $r$ is found from $6=2r\sin36^{\circ}\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{3}{\sin36^{\circ}}=5.104$. Each triangle's area $=\tfrac12\times5.104^2\times\sin72^{\circ}=\tfrac12\times26.05\times0.9511=12.39\text{ cm}^2$. Total pentagon area $=5\times12.39=61.9\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).

challenge_questions.statement: Explain, in terms of the inequality $b\sin A<a<b$, why a right angle at $A$ (i.e. $A=90^{\circ}$) can never produce a genuine ambiguous case when using the sine rule to find angle $B$ from sides $a,b$ and angle $A$.
challenge_questions.answer: When $A=90^{\circ}$, $\sin A=1$, so the condition becomes $b<a<b$, which is never true (no number is strictly greater than and strictly less than the same value $b$) — so the ambiguous window is always empty.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The ambiguous case requires $b\sin A<a<b$. Substituting $A=90^{\circ}$ gives $\sin A=1$, so the condition becomes $b\times1<a<b$, i.e. $b<a<b$. No value of $a$ can be simultaneously strictly greater than $b$ and strictly less than $b$, so this inequality is never satisfiable: a right-angled setup never produces a genuine two-solution ambiguous case (which makes sense, since a right-angled triangle with a right angle at $A$ is uniquely determined by SOH-CAH-TOA alone).

challenge_questions.statement: A triangle has sides $a,b,c$ with $a=2,b=3,c=4$ (in some unit). Find its area using the cosine rule to find one angle first, then the area formula, and verify your answer is consistent with Heron's formula $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$ where $s=\tfrac12(a+b+c)$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $\cos C=\dfrac{2^2+3^2-4^2}{2\times2\times3}=\dfrac{4+9-16}{12}=\dfrac{-3}{12}=-0.25$. $C=\cos^{-1}(-0.25)=104.48^{\circ}$. Area $=\tfrac12\times2\times3\times\sin104.48^{\circ}=3\times0.9682=2.90$. Heron's check: $s=\tfrac12(2+3+4)=4.5$; Area $=\sqrt{4.5\times2.5\times1.5\times0.5}=\sqrt{8.4375}=2.90$ — matching.

mcq.stem: Triangle $ABC$ has no right angle, with $A=50^{\circ}$, $AB=10\text{ cm}$, and $BC$ is required. Which method should be used?

options.why_wrong: SOH-CAH-TOA requires a right angle to define opposite/adjacent/hypotenuse meaningfully; with no right angle present, there is no hypotenuse to label.

options.text: Pythagoras' theorem directly on the two known sides.
options.why_wrong: Pythagoras' theorem, like SOH-CAH-TOA, applies only in a right-angled triangle; with no right angle here it cannot be used.

options.text: Trigonometry cannot be used at all, because it only works in right-angled triangles.
options.why_wrong: SOH-CAH-TOA needs a right angle, but the sine and cosine rules extend trigonometry to ANY triangle, so trigonometry can still be used here.

options.text: The sine or cosine rule, since there is no right angle to use SOH-CAH-TOA.

mcq.explanation: With no right angle present, SOH-CAH-TOA and ordinary Pythagoras do not apply; the sine or cosine rule (depending on what else is known) is the correct tool for a general triangle.

mcq.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $a=9\text{ cm}$, $b=12\text{ cm}$ and angle $A=40^{\circ}$ (not the angle between $a$ and $b$). To find angle $B$, which rule should be used?

options.text: The cosine rule's angle-finding version, $\cos B=\dfrac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2ac}$.
options.why_wrong: The cosine rule's angle-finding version needs all THREE sides; here only two sides and a non-included angle are known, which is exactly the sine rule's configuration, not the cosine rule's.
This version finds a SIDE, not an angle, and in any case requires the angle included between the two known sides, which is not what is given here.

options.text: SOH-CAH-TOA, since two sides are already known.
options.why_wrong: SOH-CAH-TOA requires a right angle, which is not stated or implied to exist in this triangle.

mcq.explanation: A complete opposite pair ($a,A$) is known, plus a second side ($b$) whose opposite angle ($B$) is sought: this is exactly the sine rule's configuration.

mcq.stem: Solving $\sin B=0.72$ as part of a sine-rule angle problem, a student finds $B_1=46.05^{\circ}$. What must be checked before accepting this as the ONLY solution?

options.text: Nothing further; a calculator's answer is always the complete solution.
options.why_wrong: A calculator's inverse sine always returns only the ACUTE solution; the obtuse supplement must be separately checked for validity in a sine-rule context, since both can represent genuine triangles.

options.text: Whether the obtuse supplement $B_2=133.95^{\circ}$ also keeps the angle sum under $180^{\circ}$ with the known angle $A$.

options.why_wrong: A calculator's $\sin^{-1}$ output is always between $0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$ by definition, so this check can never reveal anything new; the real check is on the SEPARATE obtuse supplement value.

options.text: Whether the triangle has a right angle.
options.why_wrong: The sine rule's ambiguous case can arise in ANY general triangle configuration; whether a right angle happens to be present is not the relevant check (and in fact a right angle at the known angle A rules out ambiguity entirely, as shown elsewhere in this lesson, but that is not the general check needed here).

mcq.explanation: The obtuse supplement $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$ is a genuine second solution exactly when $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$; this must always be checked when the sine rule is used to find an angle from two sides and a non-included angle.

mcq.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A=40^{\circ}$, $a=15\text{ cm}$ and $b=11\text{ cm}$. What is angle $B$?

options.why_wrong: Checking the angle sum: $A+151.9^{\circ}=40^{\circ}+151.9^{\circ}=191.9^{\circ}>180^{\circ}$, which is impossible in a triangle, so the obtuse supplement is NOT valid here; since $a>b$, angle $B$ must in fact be smaller than angle $A$, ruling out any obtuse value.
This uses the wrong inverse trigonometric function entirely; the sine rule requires $\sin^{-1}$, not $\cos^{-1}$, to extract the angle from $\sin B=0.4714$.
A valid, unique solution does exist ($B=28.1^{\circ}$); the configuration is well-defined since $a>b$ guarantees exactly one valid value of $B$.

mcq.explanation: $\sin B=\dfrac{11\sin40^{\circ}}{15}=0.4714\Rightarrow B_1=28.12^{\circ}$. Since $a(15)>b(11)$, angle $B$ must be smaller than angle $A$, which rules out the obtuse supplement: only one triangle exists.

mcq.stem: A triangle has sides $a=8\text{ cm}$, $b=11\text{ cm}$, and the angle between THEM is $38^{\circ}$. A different angle, $A=46.4^{\circ}$ (opposite $a$), is also marked on the diagram. What should be substituted into Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$ to find the area correctly?

options.why_wrong: $46.4^{\circ}$ is angle $A$, opposite side $a$, NOT the angle included between sides $a$ and $b$; substituting it does not give the triangle's area.

options.text: It cannot be found without more information.
options.why_wrong: Exactly enough information (two sides AND the angle between them, $38^{\circ}$) is already given to find the area directly; no further information is needed.
There is no need to find a third angle at all — the angle BETWEEN the two sides being used ($38^{\circ}$) is already directly given and is exactly what the formula requires.

options.text: $a=8,b=11,C=38^{\circ}$ (the angle actually between the two sides used).

mcq.explanation: The area formula $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ requires $C$ to be specifically the angle included between sides $a$ and $b$; here that is the given $38^{\circ}$, not any other angle in the diagram.

flashcards.front: The sine rule
flashcards.back: $\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}=\dfrac{c}{\sin C}$, where each lower-case side is opposite its matching upper-case angle.

flashcards.front: The cosine rule (for a side)
flashcards.back: $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$, where $A$ is the angle INCLUDED between sides $b$ and $c$.

flashcards.front: The cosine rule (for an angle)
flashcards.back: $\cos A=\dfrac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}$.

flashcards.front: Area of any triangle, given two sides and the included angle
flashcards.back: Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$, where $C$ is between sides $a$ and $b$.

flashcards.front: When to use the sine rule vs. the cosine rule
flashcards.back: Sine rule: a complete opposite pair known, plus one more piece. Cosine rule: two sides and the included angle (for a side), or all three sides (for an angle).

flashcards.front: The ambiguous-case condition
flashcards.back: With $A$ acute, two solutions for angle $B$ exist exactly when $b\sin A<a<b$ (equivalently, when $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$ for the obtuse supplement $B_2$).

flashcards.front: True or false: a calculator's sine-rule angle answer is always complete.
flashcards.back: False. It gives only the acute solution; the obtuse supplement must be checked separately for validity.

flashcards.front: Why can a negative value of $\cos A$ appear when using the cosine rule to find an angle?
flashcards.back: It is not an error — it correctly signals that angle $A$ is obtuse (greater than $90^{\circ}$), since cosine is negative for obtuse angles.

flashcards.front: Cosine rule vs. Pythagoras' theorem
flashcards.back: The cosine rule generalises Pythagoras: when the included angle is $90^{\circ}$, $\cos A=0$ and $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$ collapses exactly to $a^2=b^2+c^2$.

flashcards.front: Finding the area from three sides only
flashcards.back: First find any one angle with the rearranged cosine rule, then substitute it (and the two sides enclosing it) into Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$.

flashcards.front: Which angle is largest in a triangle?
flashcards.back: The angle opposite the LONGEST side (and the angle opposite the shortest side is the smallest).

flashcards.front: In a bearings problem with two non-perpendicular legs, what must be found before the sine/cosine rule can be applied?
flashcards.back: The interior angle at the turn point, found from the difference between the outgoing bearing and the REVERSED incoming bearing (incoming bearing $\pm180^{\circ}$).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Trying to use SOH-CAH-TOA in a triangle that has no right angle.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: SOH-CAH-TOA was the only trigonometric tool available for many lessons, so it is the first (and sometimes only) method learners reach for, even when the triangle has no $90^{\circ}$ angle at all.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner labels sides 'opposite'/'adjacent'/'hypotenuse' in a triangle where no angle is $90^{\circ}$, or writes $\sin\theta=\text{opp}/\text{hyp}$ for a general triangle.
misconceptions.correct_model: SOH-CAH-TOA is valid ONLY in a right-angled triangle. A triangle with no right angle requires the sine rule ($\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}$) or the cosine rule ($a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$) instead.
misconceptions.remediation: Make checking for a right-angle marker the compulsory first step of every triangle problem, before choosing a method.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Using the cosine rule's side-finding version when two sides and a NON-included angle are given, instead of the sine rule.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The two rules look superficially similar (both relate sides and angles of a general triangle) so it is easy to reach for the 'other' rule without checking which pieces of information are actually known.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: Given two sides and an angle NOT between them, the learner attempts $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$ even though the angle given is not the included angle.
misconceptions.correct_model: Use the cosine rule for a side ONLY when two sides AND their INCLUDED angle are known. When two angles and a side (or two sides and a non-included angle) are known, use the sine rule instead.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, explicitly label which two pieces of information are known and check: 'is the known angle between the two known sides?' If yes, cosine rule; if no, sine rule.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Missing the ambiguous case: when finding an angle with the sine rule, only reporting the acute solution and never checking whether the obtuse supplement also forms a valid triangle.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A calculator's $\sin^{-1}$ always returns the acute angle, and most triangle configurations do NOT in fact have a second valid solution, so the habit of checking is easy to skip until it matters.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: Given $A=40^{\circ},a=12,b=15$ and asked for $B$, the learner reports only $B=53.46^{\circ}$ without checking whether $B=126.54^{\circ}$ is also geometrically valid (it is, since $40^{\circ}+126.54^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$).
misconceptions.correct_model: After finding the acute angle $B_1$ from $\sin^{-1}$, always check the obtuse supplement $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$: it is a VALID second triangle exactly when $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$ (equivalently, when the side opposite the known angle, $a$, is strictly between $b\sin A$ and $b$). If $A+B_2\ge180^{\circ}$, only the acute solution is valid.
misconceptions.remediation: Make checking $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$, where $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$ (this is the same as checking $A<B_1$), a compulsory final step whenever the sine rule is used to find an angle from two sides and a non-included angle.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Using the two-side area formula $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ with an angle that is NOT the angle included between the two given sides.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The formula's three letters ($a,b,C$) can be filled in with whichever side/angle values are available without checking that $C$ is specifically the angle BETWEEN sides $a$ and $b$.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: Given sides $8$ and $11$ with the angle between a DIFFERENT pair of sides equal to $38^{\circ}$, the learner computes $\tfrac12\times8\times11\times\sin38^{\circ}$ regardless.
misconceptions.correct_model: In Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$, $C$ MUST be the angle included between the two sides $a$ and $b$ that are substituted; using a non-included angle gives a meaningless result.
misconceptions.remediation: Before substituting, explicitly trace on the diagram that the angle used sits exactly between the two sides used.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attempting SOH-CAH-TOA in a triangle with no right angle.
common_mistakes.why: SOH-CAH-TOA was the only trigonometric tool used for many prior lessons, so it is the automatic first reach even when no right angle exists.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check explicitly for a right-angle marker before choosing a method; its absence is the signal to use the sine or cosine rule.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the cosine rule's side-finding version when the known angle is not the included one.
common_mistakes.why: The two rules look similar, so it is tempting to use whichever one 'has the most known values plugged in' without checking the included-angle condition.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before calculating, explicitly check: is the known angle positioned BETWEEN the two known sides? If not, use the sine rule.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting only the acute angle from a sine-rule calculation without checking for a valid obtuse second solution.
common_mistakes.why: A calculator's $\sin^{-1}$ always gives the acute value, and the habit of checking the obtuse supplement is easy to skip since most configurations do not actually need it.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Make checking $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$ (where $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$) a compulsory final step whenever the sine rule is used to find an angle this way.

exam_notes: Before choosing a rule, explicitly identify: is there a right angle (use SOH-CAH-TOA/Pythagoras)? A complete opposite pair plus one more piece (sine rule)? Two sides and the included angle, or three sides (cosine rule)?
A negative value of $\cos A$ when using the cosine rule for an angle is a completely normal, valid result indicating an obtuse angle; do not 'correct' it to positive.

Whenever the sine rule is used to find an angle from two sides and a non-included angle, state explicitly whether the obtuse alternative is possible (check $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$), even if the answer turns out to be a single value; this shows the examiner you have considered the ambiguous case.
In the area formula Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$, always verify that $C$ is the angle actually included between the two sides $a$ and $b$ being substituted.

summary.big_idea: Any triangle, not just a right-angled one, can be solved using the sine rule (a complete opposite pair plus one more piece) or the cosine rule (two sides and the included angle, or all three sides); the sine rule can occasionally produce TWO valid triangles (the ambiguous case), which must always be checked for when finding an angle this way.
key_points: Sine rule: $\dfrac{a}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b}{\sin B}=\dfrac{c}{\sin C}$ — needs a complete opposite pair plus one more piece of information.
Cosine rule (side): $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$ — needs two sides and the INCLUDED angle.
Cosine rule (angle): $\cos A=\dfrac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}$ — needs all three sides; a negative result means $A$ is obtuse.
Area $=\tfrac12ab\sin C$ — needs two sides and the angle between them.

The ambiguous case: when finding an angle with the sine rule from two sides and a non-included angle, always check whether the obtuse supplement $B_2=180^{\circ}-B_1$ also satisfies $A+B_2<180^{\circ}$.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: No right angle: use the sine rule (complete opposite pair known) or cosine rule (two sides + included angle, or three sides); when the sine rule finds an angle from two sides and a non-included angle, always check the obtuse supplement for a second valid triangle before finalising the answer.
