exercises.statement: Triangle PQR has a right angle at Q, angle $P=42°$, and adjacent side $PQ=6$ cm. Calculate the opposite side QR.
exercises.full_solution: $\tan42° = \dfrac{QR}{6} \Rightarrow QR = 6\tan42° = 5.4024\ldots = 5.40$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangle XYZ has a right angle at Y, angle $X=35°$, and opposite side $YZ=6$ cm. Calculate the adjacent side XY.
exercises.full_solution: $\tan35° = \dfrac{6}{XY} \Rightarrow XY = \dfrac{6}{\tan35°} = 8.5689\ldots = 8.57$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use the tangent ratio to calculate the length $x$ cm marked in each right-angled triangle (angle, adjacent/opposite side given): (a) angle $20°$, adjacent side $5$ cm, $x$ = opposite side; (b) angle $30°$, adjacent side $7$ cm, $x$ = opposite side; (c) angle $58°$, adjacent side $12$ cm, $x$ = opposite side; (d) angle $18°$, adjacent side $15$ cm, $x$ = opposite side; (e) angle $75°$, adjacent side $10$ cm, $x$ = opposite side; (f) angle $60°$, adjacent side $8$ cm, $x$ = opposite side.
exercises.full_solution:
In each part $x=\text{adjacent}\times\tan(\text{angle})$ since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.

(a) $x=5\tan20°=1.820$ cm.

(b) $x=7\tan30°=4.041$ cm.

(c) $x=12\tan58°=19.204$ cm.

(d) $x=15\tan18°=4.874$ cm.

(e) $x=10\tan75°=37.321$ cm.

(f) $x=8\tan60°=13.856$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use the tangent ratio to calculate the length $x$ cm (adjacent side) in each right-angled triangle: (a) angle $40°$, opposite side $12$ cm; (b) angle $38°$, opposite side $7$ cm; (c) angle $65°$, opposite side $20$ cm; (d) angle $26°$, opposite side $2$ cm; (e) angle $25°$, opposite side $6.5$ cm; (f) angle $56°$, opposite side $9.2$ cm.
exercises.full_solution:
In each part, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{x}\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\tan\theta}$.

(a) $x=12/\tan40°=14.301$ cm.

(b) $x=7/\tan38°=8.960$ cm.

(c) $x=20/\tan65°=9.326$ cm.

(d) $x=2/\tan26°=4.101$ cm.

(e) $x=6.5/\tan25°=13.939$ cm.

(f) $x=9.2/\tan56°=6.205$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangle ABC has a right angle at B, hypotenuse $AC=12$ cm and opposite side $BC=7$ cm. Calculate angle BAC.
exercises.full_solution: $\sin x = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{7}{12}$, so $x=\sin^{-1}(7/12)=35.7°$ (1 d.p.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangle PQR has a right angle at Q, angle $R=18°$, and opposite side $PQ=11$ cm. Calculate the hypotenuse PR.
exercises.full_solution: $\sin18° = \dfrac{11}{q}\Rightarrow q=\dfrac{11}{\sin18°}=35.6$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use the sine ratio to calculate the length of the marked side in each right-angled triangle: (a) right angle at M, angle $L=24°$, hypotenuse $LN=6$ cm, find opposite side $l=MN$; (b) right angle at Q, angle $R=60°$, hypotenuse $RP=q$, opposite side $QP=16$ cm, find hypotenuse $q$; (c) right angle at C, angle $B=49°$, opposite side $AC=8.2$ cm, find hypotenuse $c=AB$; (d) right angle at X, angle $Y=55°$, hypotenuse $YZ=2$ cm, find opposite side $y=XZ$; (e) right angle at K, angle $J=22°$, opposite side $KL=16.4$ cm, find hypotenuse $k=JL$; (f) right angle at A, angle $C=45°$, hypotenuse $BC=45$ cm, find opposite side $c=AB$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $\sin24° = \dfrac{l}{6} \Rightarrow l = 6\sin24° = 2.440$ cm.

(b) $\sin60° = \dfrac{16}{q} \Rightarrow q = \dfrac{16}{\sin60°} = 18.475$ cm.

(c) $\sin49° = \dfrac{8.2}{c} \Rightarrow c = \dfrac{8.2}{\sin49°} = 10.865$ cm.

(d) $\sin55° = \dfrac{y}{2} \Rightarrow y = 2\sin55° = 1.638$ cm.

(e) $\sin22° = \dfrac{16.4}{k} \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{16.4}{\sin22°} = 43.779$ cm.

(f) $\sin45° = \dfrac{c}{45} \Rightarrow c = 45\sin45° = 31.820$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangle XYZ has a right angle at Y, angle $X=62°$, hypotenuse $XZ=20$ cm. Calculate the adjacent side XY.
exercises.full_solution: $\cos62° = \dfrac{z}{20} \Rightarrow z=20\cos62°=9.39$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangle ABC has a right angle at C, hypotenuse $AB=12$ m, adjacent side $BC=5.3$ m (adjacent to angle B). Calculate angle ABC.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use the cosine ratio to calculate the marked side or angle in each right-angled triangle (hypotenuse always given or required): (a) angle $C=26°$, hypotenuse $AC=40$ cm, find adjacent side $a=BC$; (b) angle $X=15°$, adjacent side $XY=14.6$ cm, find hypotenuse $y=XZ$; (c) angle $x°$ at E, adjacent $EF=12$ cm, hypotenuse $GE=18$ cm, find $x$; (d) angle $a°$ at M, adjacent $LM=8.1$ cm, hypotenuse $MN=52.3$ cm, find $a$; (e) angle $Y=56°$, hypotenuse $YZ=12$ cm, find adjacent $z=XY$; (f) angle $J=27°$, adjacent $JI=15$ cm, find hypotenuse $i=HJ$; (g) angle $e°$ at X, adjacent $XY=0.2$ m, hypotenuse $XZ=0.6$ m, find $e$; (h) angle $B=81°$, hypotenuse $BA=13.7$ cm, find adjacent $a=BC$.
exercises.full_solution:
Using $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ in each right triangle:

(a) $a=40\cos26°=35.952$ cm.

(b) $y=14.6/\cos15°=15.115$ cm.

(c) $\cos x=12/18 \Rightarrow x=\cos^{-1}(2/3)=48.190°$.

(d) $\cos a=8.1/52.3 \Rightarrow a=\cos^{-1}(8.1/52.3)=81.090°$.

(e) $z=12\cos56°=6.710$ cm.

(f) $i=15/\cos27°=16.835$ cm.

(g) $\cos e=0.2/0.6=1/3 \Rightarrow e=\cos^{-1}(1/3)=70.529°$.

(h) $a=13.7\cos81°=2.143$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Right triangle ABC, right angle at A, $AB=6$ m, $AC=8$ m. Calculate BC.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Right triangle ABC, right angle at C, $AB=12$ m (hypotenuse), $BC=5$ m. Calculate AC.
exercises.full_solution: $a^2=b^2+c^2 \Rightarrow 12^2=b^2+5^2 \Rightarrow b^2=144-25=119 \Rightarrow b=\sqrt{119}=10.9$ m (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use Pythagoras' theorem to calculate the length of the marked side in each right-angled triangle: (a) legs $4$ cm, $3$ cm, hypotenuse $a$; (b) legs $9$ mm, $7$ mm, hypotenuse $b$; (c) leg $9$ cm, hypotenuse $15$ cm, other leg $c$; (d) leg $15$ cm, hypotenuse $20$ cm, other leg $d$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: For each composite figure made of right-angled triangles sharing a side, use Pythagoras' theorem (possibly twice) to find the marked length: (a) a right-angled triangle has legs $9$ cm (vertical) and $5$ cm (base); a second right-angled triangle is built on its hypotenuse, with the right angle at the top of the $9$ cm side and a second leg of $4$ cm; find the hypotenuse $e$ of this second triangle. (b) a right-angled triangle has legs $12$ cm (vertical) and $5$ cm (top side); a second right-angled triangle is built on its hypotenuse, with the right angle at the end of the $5$ cm side and a second leg of $7$ cm; find the hypotenuse $f$ of this second triangle. (c) a right-angled triangle has a vertical side of $8$ cm and hypotenuse $16$ cm; a line of length $10$ cm is drawn from the top vertex to a point on the base; $g$ is the part of the base between that point and the acute angle at the far end. (d) a straight base line L-M-R with $LM=3$ cm, $MR=6$ cm, and apex N below M with $MN\perp LR$; $NR=9$ cm; find $h=NL$. (e) a 'spiral' of right-angled triangles sharing a common vertex: the first has legs $1$ cm and $1$ cm; each new triangle uses the previous hypotenuse as one leg, and its outer leg is marked ($\sqrt2$ cm for the second triangle, $\sqrt5$ cm for the third); find the hypotenuse $j$ of the third triangle. (f) a quadrilateral with a right angle at the bottom-left vertex, left side $4$ cm, right side $12$ cm (both vertical, and horizontal top/bottom); one diagonal is $8$ cm; find the other diagonal $k$.
exercises.answer: (a) $e=\sqrt{122}\approx11.0$ cm (b) $f=\sqrt{218}\approx14.8$ cm (c) $g=8\sqrt3-6\approx7.86$ cm (d) $h=3\sqrt6\approx7.35$ cm (e) $j=3$ cm (f) $k=8\sqrt3\approx13.9$ cm
exercises.full_solution:
(a) First find the shared side (the hypotenuse of the first triangle): $\sqrt{9^2+5^2}=\sqrt{106}$ cm. This is a leg of the second right-angled triangle, whose other leg is $4$ cm, so $e=\sqrt{106+4^2}=\sqrt{122}=11.045$ cm.

(b) Shared side: $\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=\sqrt{169}=13$ cm. In the second right-angled triangle the legs are $13$ cm and $7$ cm, so $f=\sqrt{13^2+7^2}=\sqrt{218}=14.765$ cm.

(c) Whole base of the large right-angled triangle: $\sqrt{16^2-8^2}=\sqrt{192}=13.856$ cm. Base of the smaller right-angled triangle (hypotenuse $10$, vertical side $8$): $\sqrt{10^2-8^2}=6$ cm. So $g=13.856-6=7.856$ cm.

(d) In right triangle $MNR$: $MN=\sqrt{9^2-6^2}=\sqrt{45}$. Then in right triangle $LMN$: $h=\sqrt{3^2+45}=\sqrt{54}=3\sqrt6=7.348$ cm.

(e) First hypotenuse: $\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2$ cm. Second: $\sqrt{(\sqrt2)^2+(\sqrt2)^2}=\sqrt4=2$ cm. Third: $j=\sqrt{2^2+(\sqrt5)^2}=\sqrt9=3$ cm.

(f) Let the top/bottom width be $w$. With bottom-left at $(0,0)$: bottom-right $(w,0)$, top-left $(0,4)$, top-right $(w,12)$. The diagonal bottom-right-to-top-left $=8$: $\sqrt{w^2+16}=8\Rightarrow w^2=48$. The other diagonal $k=$ bottom-left-to-top-right $=\sqrt{w^2+144}=\sqrt{48+144}=\sqrt{192}=8\sqrt3=13.856$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two trees stand on flat ground. The height of the smaller tree is $7$ m. The distance between the top of the smaller tree and the base of the taller tree is $15$ m. The distance between the top of the taller tree and the base of the smaller tree is $20$ m. Calculate (a) the horizontal distance between the two trees, (b) the height of the taller tree.
exercises.full_solution:
Let the horizontal distance between the trees be $d$ and the height of the taller tree be $H$.

From the right triangle formed by the smaller tree's top, its base... using the top of the small tree (height 7) to the base of the tall tree (horizontal distance $d$): $d^2+7^2=15^2 \Rightarrow d^2=225-49=176 \Rightarrow d=\sqrt{176}=13.27$ m.

From the top of the tall tree (height $H$) to the base of the small tree: $d^2+H^2=20^2 \Rightarrow H^2=400-176=224 \Rightarrow H=\sqrt{224}=14.97$ m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using Pythagoras' theorem, trigonometry, or both, calculate the marked value in each diagram, to 1 d.p.: (a) right angle at B, $AB=6$ cm, hypotenuse $AC=8.7$ cm, find angle $x$ at C; (b) right angle at K, angle $J=38°$, opposite side $KL=15.2$ cm, find adjacent side $JK=l$; (c) right angle at N, legs $LN=4.8$ cm, $MN=l$, hypotenuse $LM=17.4$ cm, find $l$; (d) right angle at X, adjacent side $XY=14$ cm, hypotenuse $YZ=19$ cm, find angle $z$ at Y.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A sailing boat sets off from point X and heads towards Y, a point $17$ km north. At Y, it changes direction and heads towards Z, a point $12$ km away on a bearing of $090°$. Once at Z, the crew want to sail back to X. Calculate (a) the distance ZX, (b) the bearing of X from Z.
exercises.full_solution:
Take X as the origin. $Y=(0,17)$. Since the bearing from Y to Z is $090°$ (due east), $Z=Y+(12,0)=(12,17)$.

$ZX=\sqrt{12^2+17^2}=\sqrt{433}=20.81$ km.

Bearing of X from Z: vector $Z\to X=(-12,-17)$, which lies in the south-west quadrant. Bearing $=180°+\tan^{-1}(12/17)=215.2°\approx215°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: An aeroplane sets off from G on a bearing of $024°$ towards H, a point $250$ km away. At H, it changes course and heads towards J, which is $180$ km away on a bearing of $055°$. Calculate (a) how far H is to the north of G, (b) how far H is to the east of G, (c) how far J is to the north of H, (d) how far J is to the east of H, (e) the shortest distance between G and J, (f) the bearing of G from J.
exercises.answer: (a) $\approx228.4$ km (b) $\approx101.7$ km (c) $\approx103.2$ km (d) $\approx147.4$ km (e) $\approx414.8$ km (f) bearing $\approx217°$
exercises.full_solution:
(a) North component $=250\cos24°=228.39$ km.

(b) East component $=250\sin24°=101.68$ km.

(c) North component $=180\cos55°=103.24$ km.

(d) East component $=180\sin55°=147.45$ km.

(e) Total: J is $(249.13)$ km east and $(331.63)$ km north of G. $GJ=\sqrt{(249.13)^2+(331.63)^2}=414.8$ km.

(f) The bearing of G from J is the direction of the vector J$\to$G $=(-249.13,-331.63)$ (south-west quadrant): bearing $=180+\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{249.13}{331.63}\right)=216.9°\approx217°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two trees are standing on flat ground. The angle of elevation of their tops from a point X on the ground is $40°$ (X, the top of the small tree, and the top of the tall tree are collinear). The horizontal distance between X and the small tree is $8$ m, and the distance between the tops of the two trees is $20$ m. Calculate (a) the height of the small tree, (b) the height of the tall tree, (c) the horizontal distance between the trees.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) height of small tree $=8\tan40°=6.71$ m.

(c) Since X, and both tree-tops are collinear at elevation $40°$, the horizontal gap $d$ between the trees satisfies (distance between tops) $=\dfrac{d}{\cos40°}=20 \Rightarrow d=20\cos40°=15.32$ m.

(b) height of tall tree $=(8+d)\tan40°=(8+15.32)\tan40°=19.57$ m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: PQRS is a quadrilateral. Sides RS and QR are equal in length ($9$ cm each). Sides QP and RS are parallel. Diagonal $SQ=12$ cm, and angle $SPQ=90°$. Calculate (a) angle SQR, (b) angle PSQ, (c) length PQ, (d) length PS, (e) the area of PQRS.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Triangle QRS is isosceles ($QR=RS=9$), base $SQ=12$. Dropping a perpendicular from R to SQ bisects it, giving a right triangle with hypotenuse $9$ and adjacent half-base $6$: $\angle SQR=\cos^{-1}(6/9)=48.19°$ (this equals the base angle at S too, $\angle QSR$, by isosceles symmetry).

(b) Since $QP\parallel RS$ and $SQ$ is a transversal, $\angle PQS=\angle QSR=48.19°$ (alternate angles). In right triangle $SPQ$ (right angle at P), $\angle PSQ=90°-\angle PQS=41.81°$.

(c) $PQ=SQ\cos(\angle PQS)=12\cos(48.19°)=8.00$ cm (exactly $8$ cm, since $\cos(\angle PQS)=2/3$).

(d) $PS=SQ\sin(\angle PQS)=12\sin(48.19°)=8.944$ cm.

(e) Area of $\triangle SQR=\tfrac12\times12\times h$ where $h=\sqrt{9^2-6^2}=\sqrt{45}$, giving $40.25$ cm$^2$. Area of $\triangle SPQ=\tfrac12\times PQ\times PS=35.78$ cm$^2$. Total area $=76.0$ cm$^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The base of a tower is $60$ m away from a point X on the ground. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from X is $40°$. Calculate the height of the tower, to the nearest metre.
exercises.full_solution: $\tan40°=\dfrac{h}{60} \Rightarrow h=60\tan40°=50.3$ m $\approx50$ m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (angle of elevation, tower height)

exercises.statement: An aeroplane receives a signal from a point X on the ground. The angle of depression of point X from the aeroplane is $30°$, and the line-of-sight distance from the aeroplane to X is $6$ km. Calculate the height at which the plane is flying, to the nearest $0.1$ km.
exercises.full_solution: $\sin30°=\dfrac{h}{6} \Rightarrow h=6\sin30°=3.0$ km.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (angle of depression, aeroplane height)

exercises.statement: A and B are two villages. The horizontal distance between them is $12$ km and the vertical distance between them is $2$ km. Calculate (a) the shortest distance between the two villages, (b) the angle of elevation of B from A.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) By Pythagoras: distance $=\sqrt{12^2+2^2}=\sqrt{148}=12.166$ km.

(b) $\tan\theta=2/12 \Rightarrow \theta=\tan^{-1}(2/12)=9.462°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: X and Y are two towns. The horizontal distance between them is $10$ km and the angle of depression of Y from X is $7°$. Calculate (a) the shortest distance between the two towns, (b) the vertical height between the two towns.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $\cos7°=\dfrac{10}{d} \Rightarrow d=\dfrac{10}{\cos7°}=10.075$ km.

(b) $\tan7°=\dfrac{v}{10} \Rightarrow v=10\tan7°=1.228$ km.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A girl standing on a hill at A can see a small boat at a point B on a lake. The girl is at a height of $50$ m above B and at a horizontal distance of $120$ m away from B. Calculate (a) the angle of depression of the boat from the girl, (b) the shortest distance between the girl and the boat.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $\tan\theta=50/120 \Rightarrow \theta=\tan^{-1}(50/120)=22.620°$ (the angle of depression equals this angle of elevation, by alternate angles).

(b) By Pythagoras: distance $=\sqrt{50^2+120^2}=\sqrt{16900}=130$ m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two hot air balloons are $1$ km apart in the air. The angle of elevation of the higher balloon from the lower balloon is $20°$. Calculate, to the nearest metre, (a) the vertical height between the two balloons, (b) the horizontal distance between the two balloons.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using binoculars, three people, P, Q and R, can see each other across a valley. P, Q and R lie in the same vertical plane, with Q at the bottom of the valley and P, R on higher ground at either side. The horizontal distance between P and Q is $6.8$ km and the horizontal distance between Q and R is $10$ km. The shortest (straight-line) distance between P and Q is $7$ km, and the angle of depression of Q from R is $15°$. Calculate (a) the vertical height between Q and R, (b) the vertical height between P and R, (c) the angle of elevation of R from P, (d) the shortest distance between P and R.
exercises.full_solution:
First, the vertical height between P and Q (needed for part (b)): by Pythagoras, $v_{PQ}=\sqrt{7^2-6.8^2}=\sqrt{2.76}=1.661$ km (height of P above Q).

(a) Using the angle of depression of Q from R ($15°$) with horizontal distance $QR=10$ km: $v_{QR}=10\tan15°=2.679$ km (height of R above Q).

(b) Height of R above P $=v_{QR}-v_{PQ}=2.679-1.661=1.018$ km.

(c) Total horizontal distance P to R $=6.8+10=16.8$ km. $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1.018}{16.8}\right)=3.468°$.

(d) By Pythagoras: $PR=\sqrt{16.8^2+1.018^2}=16.831$ km.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two people, A and B, are standing either side of a transmission mast. A is $130$ m away from the mast and B is $200$ m away. The angle of elevation of the top of the mast from A is $60°$. Calculate (a) the height of the mast, to the nearest metre, (b) the angle of elevation of the top of the mast from B.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $\tan60°=\dfrac{h}{130} \Rightarrow h=130\tan60°=225.17$ m $\approx 225$ m.

(b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{h}{200}=\dfrac{225.17}{200} \Rightarrow \theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{225.17}{200}\right)=48.388°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $\sin30°=0.5$. Which other angle between $0°$ and $180°$ has a sine of $0.5$?
exercises.full_solution: From the symmetry of the sine curve about $x=90°$: $\sin x=\sin(180°-x)$. So the other angle is $180°-30°=150°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express each of the following in terms of the sine of another angle between $0°$ and $180°$: (a) $\sin60°$ (b) $\sin80°$ (c) $\sin115°$ (d) $\sin140°$ (e) $\sin128°$ (f) $\sin167°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express each of the following in terms of the sine of another angle between $0°$ and $180°$: (a) $\sin35°$ (b) $\sin50°$ (c) $\sin30°$ (d) $\sin48°$ (e) $\sin104°$ (f) $\sin127°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the two angles between $0°$ and $180°$ which have the following sine (give each angle to the nearest degree): (a) $0.33$ (b) $0.99$ (c) $0.09$ (d) $0.95$ (e) $0.22$ (f) $0.47$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the two angles between $0°$ and $180°$ which have the following sine (give each angle to the nearest degree): (a) $0.94$ (b) $0.16$ (c) $0.80$ (d) $0.56$ (e) $0.28$ (f) $0.33$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: $\cos60°=0.5$. Which angle between $0°$ and $180°$ has a cosine of $-0.5$?
exercises.full_solution: From the symmetry of the cosine curve: $\cos x°=-\cos(180-x)°$. Reading the graph, $\cos120°=-0.5$, so $\cos60°=-\cos120°$. The required angle is $120°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The cosine of which angle between $0°$ and $180°$ is equal to the negative of $\cos50°$?
exercises.full_solution: Using $\cos x°=-\cos(180-x)°$ with $x=50$: $-\cos50°=\cos(180-50)°=\cos130°$. So $\cos130°=-\cos50°$, and the required angle is $130°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express each of the following in terms of the cosine of another angle between $0°$ and $180°$: (a) $\cos20°$ (b) $\cos85°$ (c) $\cos32°$ (d) $\cos95°$ (e) $\cos147°$ (f) $\cos106°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express each of the following in terms of the cosine of another angle between $0°$ and $180°$: (a) $\cos98°$ (b) $\cos144°$ (c) $\cos160°$ (d) $\cos143°$ (e) $\cos171°$ (f) $\cos123°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Express each of the following in terms of the cosine of another angle between $0°$ and $180°$: (a) $-\cos100°$ (b) $\cos90°$ (c) $-\cos110°$ (d) $-\cos45°$ (e) $-\cos122°$ (f) $-\cos25°$.
exercises.full_solution: Using $-\cos x°=\cos(180-x)°$ (the same identity rearranged): (a) $180-100=80$. (b) $\cos90°=0$ exactly, a special case ($90°$ maps to itself since $180-90=90$). (c) $180-110=70$. (d) $180-45=135$. (e) $180-122=58$. (f) $180-25=155$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Write each expression as the cosine of an acute angle: (a) $-\cos125^{\circ}$ (b) $-\cos107^{\circ}$ (c) $-\cos120^{\circ}$ (d) $-\cos98^{\circ}$ (e) $-\cos92^{\circ}$ (f) $-\cos110^{\circ}$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Explain, with reference to a right-angled triangle, why the tangent of $90°$ is undefined.
exercises.answer: $\tan90°$ is undefined because it requires division by zero.
exercises.full_solution: In a right-angled triangle, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$. As $\theta\to90°$, the triangle degenerates: the side adjacent to $\theta$ shrinks towards zero length while the opposite side approaches the hypotenuse. Since $\tan90°$ would require dividing by an adjacent side of length $0$, the ratio is undefined (it is consistent with the tangent graph, which has a vertical asymptote at $x=90°$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Angle $A$ is an obtuse angle. If $\sin A=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, calculate the size of $A$.
exercises.full_solution: $A=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=60°$ from a calculator. Since $A$ must be obtuse ($90°<A<180°$), $A\neq60°$. By the symmetry of the sine curve, $\sin60°=\sin120°$, so $A=120°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (solving trig equations, obtuse angle)

exercises.statement: If $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, calculate the possible values for $\theta$ in the range $0\le\theta\le360$.
exercises.full_solution: $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)=30°$. Since $y=\tan\theta$ has period $180°$, another solution in range is $30°+180°=210°$. So $\theta=30°,210°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (solving trig equations, tan over 0°-360°)

exercises.statement: Solve each of the following equations, giving all the solutions in the range $0\le\theta\le360$: (a) $\sin\theta=\dfrac14$ (b) $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ (c) $\sin\theta=-\dfrac12$ (d) $\tan\theta=-\sqrt3$ (e) $5\cos\theta+1=2$ (f) $\dfrac12\tan\theta+2=1$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.25)=14.478°$; other solution $=180-14.478=165.522°$.

(b) $\theta=\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt2)=45°$; cosine is also positive in the 4th quadrant: $\theta=360-45=315°$.

(c) Reference angle $=\sin^{-1}(0.5)=30°$. Sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants: $\theta=180+30=210°$ and $\theta=360-30=330°$.

(d) Reference angle $=\tan^{-1}(\sqrt3)=60°$. Tangent is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants: $\theta=180-60=120°$ and $\theta=360-60=300°$.

(e) $5\cos\theta+1=2 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=0.2 \Rightarrow \theta=\cos^{-1}(0.2)=78.463°$; other solution $=360-78.463=281.537°$ (cosine also positive in 4th quadrant).

(f) $\tfrac12\tan\theta+2=1 \Rightarrow \tan\theta=-2$. Reference angle $=\tan^{-1}(2)=63.435°$. Tangent negative in 2nd, 4th quadrants: $\theta=180-63.435=116.565°$ and $\theta=360-63.435=296.565°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In a right-angled triangle, the angle $\theta$ is such that $\tan\theta=\dfrac34$ (the side opposite $\theta$ is $3$ and the side adjacent is $4$). Deduce, without a calculator, the value of (a) $\sin\theta$ (b) $\cos\theta$.
exercises.full_solution: Since $\tan\theta=3/4$, the triangle has legs $3$ and $4$; by Pythagoras the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$ (a 3-4-5 triangle). So $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac35$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac45$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In a right-angled triangle, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{3}{10}$ (the side opposite $\theta$ is $3$ and the hypotenuse is $10$). Deduce, without a calculator, the exact value of (a) $\cos\theta$ (b) $\tan\theta$.
exercises.full_solution: By Pythagoras, the side adjacent to $\theta$ is $\sqrt{10^2-3^2}=\sqrt{91}$. So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{91}}{10}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{91}}=\dfrac{3\sqrt{91}}{91}$ (rationalised).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using a right-angled triangle labelled with Hypotenuse, Opposite and Adjacent sides and angle $\theta$, explain why the equation $\sin\theta=\cos\theta$ occurs when $\theta=45°$.
exercises.full_solution: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{Adjacent}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}$, so $\sin\theta=\cos\theta$ exactly when Opposite $=$ Adjacent, i.e. when the right-angled triangle is isosceles. This occurs precisely when the two non-right angles are equal, i.e. both equal to $45°$ (since they sum to $90°$). Since $\sin\theta$ is increasing and $\cos\theta$ is decreasing on $0°<\theta<90°$, they cross exactly once, confirming $\theta=45°$ is the unique solution in this range.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Triangle ABC has $AB=7$ cm, $AC=9$ cm, and angle $A=50°$. Calculate the length of side BC.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (cosine rule, find a side)

exercises.statement: Triangle ABC has $BC=20$ cm (opposite $A$), $AC=15$ cm, $AB=12$ cm. Calculate the size of angle A.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (cosine rule, find an angle)

exercises.statement: Use the cosine rule to calculate the length of the side marked $x$ in each triangle: (a) two sides $2$ m and $3$ m enclosing an angle of $140°$; (b) two sides $6$ cm and $10$ cm enclosing an angle of $95°$; (c) two sides $7$ cm and $15$ cm enclosing an angle of $25°$; (d) two sides, each $4$ cm (marked equal with tick marks), enclosing an angle of $45°$; (e) two sides $5$ cm and $7$ cm enclosing an angle of $125°$. In each case $x$ is the side opposite the given angle.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Use the cosine rule to calculate the angle marked $\theta°$ in each triangle (in each case $\theta$ is enclosed between the two given sides, opposite the third given side): (a) sides $20$ m and $25$ m enclosing $\theta$, opposite side $40$ m; (b) sides $2$ mm and $4$ mm enclosing $\theta$, opposite side $5$ mm; (c) an isosceles triangle in which $\theta$ is enclosed between a side of $9$ cm and a side of $15$ cm, and the side opposite $\theta$ is also $9$ cm (tick-marked equal to the other $9$ cm side); (d) sides $4$ cm and $18$ cm enclosing $\theta$, opposite side $15$ cm; (e) sides $7$ cm and $10$ cm enclosing $\theta$, opposite side $15$ cm.
exercises.full_solution:
Using $\cos\theta=\dfrac{p^2+q^2-r^2}{2pq}$ for enclosing sides $p,q$ and opposite side $r$:

(a) $\cos\theta=(20^2+25^2-40^2)/(2\cdot20\cdot25)=-0.575 \Rightarrow \theta=125.100°$.

(b) $\cos\theta=(2^2+4^2-5^2)/(2\cdot2\cdot4)=-0.3125 \Rightarrow \theta=108.210°$.

(c) $\cos\theta=(9^2+15^2-9^2)/(2\cdot9\cdot15)=225/270=0.8333 \Rightarrow \theta=33.557°$.

(d) $\cos\theta=(4^2+18^2-15^2)/(2\cdot4\cdot18)=0.7986 \Rightarrow \theta=37.002°$.

(e) $\cos\theta=(7^2+10^2-15^2)/(2\cdot7\cdot10)=-0.5429 \Rightarrow \theta=122.878°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Four players, W, X, Y and Z, are on a rugby pitch. In plan view, quadrilateral WXYZ (in that order) has $WX=20$ m, $XY=24$ m, $YZ=40$ m, $ZW=30$ m, and angle $XYZ=80°$. The diagonal XZ is drawn. Calculate (a) the distance between players X and Z, (b) angle ZWX, (c) angle WZX, (d) angle YZX, (e) the distance between players W and Y.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) In triangle XYZ: $XZ^2=24^2+40^2-2(24)(40)\cos80°=2176-1920(0.1736)=1842.6 \Rightarrow XZ=42.925$ m.

(b) In triangle XZW (sides $XW=20$, $ZW=30$, $XZ=42.925$): $\cos(\angle ZWX)=(20^2+30^2-XZ^2)/(2\cdot20\cdot30)=-0.4522 \Rightarrow \angle ZWX=116.883°$.

(c) $\cos(\angle WZX)=(30^2+XZ^2-20^2)/(2\cdot30\cdot XZ)=0.9096 \Rightarrow \angle WZX=24.555°$.

(d) In triangle XYZ: $\cos(\angle YZX)=(40^2+XZ^2-24^2)/(2\cdot40\cdot XZ)=0.8348 \Rightarrow \angle YZX=33.409°$.

(e) $\angle WZY=\angle WZX+\angle YZX=24.555+33.409=57.965°$. Then in triangle WZY: $WY^2=30^2+40^2-2(30)(40)\cos(57.965°)=1226.94 \Rightarrow WY=35.028$ m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Three yachts, A, B and C, are racing. $AB=220$ m, $AC=450$ m, and angle $BAC=55°$. Calculate the distance between B and C, to the nearest $10$ m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two trees stand on one side of a river bank. On the opposite side, a boy stands at X. The distance from X to the base of one tree is $40$ m and to the base of the other tree is $50$ m; the angle at X between these two lines of sight is $110°$. Calculate the distance between the two trees.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the area of each triangle, using $\text{area}=\tfrac12ab\sin C$: (a) two sides $20$ cm and $14$ cm enclosing $30°$; (b) two sides $12$ mm and $12$ mm enclosing $80°$; (c) two sides $40$ cm and $35$ cm enclosing $10°$; (d) two sides $6$ cm and $8$ cm enclosing $135°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the value of $x$ in each of the following: (a) a triangle with sides $12$ cm and $16$ cm enclosing an angle $x°$, area $=40$ cm$^2$; (b) a triangle with sides $9$ cm and $x$ cm enclosing an angle of $160°$, area $=20$ cm$^2$; (c) a triangle with sides $15$ cm and $x$ cm enclosing an angle of $60°$, area $=150$ cm$^2$; (d) a triangle with sides $8$ cm and $14$ cm enclosing an angle $x°$, area $=50$ cm$^2$.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $40=\tfrac12(12)(16)\sin x=96\sin x \Rightarrow \sin x=40/96=0.4167 \Rightarrow x=24.624°$.

(b) $20=\tfrac12(9)(x)\sin160° \Rightarrow x=20/(4.5\sin160°)=12.9947$ cm.

(c) $150=\tfrac12(15)(x)\sin60° \Rightarrow x=150/(7.5\sin60°)=23.0940$ cm.

(d) $50=\tfrac12(8)(14)\sin x=56\sin x \Rightarrow \sin x=50/56=0.8929 \Rightarrow x=63.234°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A straight stretch of coast AB is shown. A ship S at sea is $1.1$ km from A. If angle $SAB=25°$, calculate the shortest distance between the ship and the coast, to the nearest metre.
exercises.full_solution: The shortest distance from S to the line AB is the perpendicular distance, $=SA\sin(\angle SAB)=1.1\times\sin25°=0.46488$ km $=464.9$ m $\approx 465$ m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: ABCDEFGH is a cube of edge length $3$ cm (top face ABCD, bottom face EFGH, with vertical edges AE, BF, CG, DH). Calculate (a) the length EG (a diagonal of the base), (b) the length AG (a space diagonal of the cube), (c) the angle EGA.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Triangle EHG is right-angled at H: $EG^2=EH^2+HG^2=3^2+3^2=18 \Rightarrow EG=\sqrt{18}=4.24$ cm.

(b) Triangle AEG is right-angled at E (AE is vertical, EG is horizontal): $AG^2=AE^2+EG^2=3^2+(\sqrt{18})^2=9+18=27 \Rightarrow AG=\sqrt{27}=5.20$ cm.

(c) In right triangle EGA (right angle at E): $\tan(\angle EGA)=\dfrac{AE}{EG}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{18}} \Rightarrow \angle EGA=35.3°$ (1 d.p.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (3D trigonometry in a cube)

exercises.statement: ABCDEFGH is a cube of edge length $4$ cm (top face ABCD, bottom face EFGH, vertical edges AE, BF, CG, DH). Calculate (a) the length HF (diagonal of the base), (b) the length HB (space diagonal), (c) the angle BHG.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $HF=\sqrt{4^2+4^2}=\sqrt{32}=5.657$ cm.

(b) $HB=\sqrt{HF^2+BF^2}=\sqrt{32+16}=\sqrt{48}=6.928$ cm.

(c) In triangle BHG: $HG=4$, $HB=6.928$, and $GB$ (face diagonal of BCGF) $=\sqrt{4^2+4^2}=5.657$. By the cosine rule: $\cos(\angle BHG)=\dfrac{HG^2+HB^2-GB^2}{2\cdot HG\cdot HB}=\dfrac{16+48-32}{2(4)(6.928)}=0.5774 \Rightarrow \angle BHG=54.736°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: ABCDEFGH is a cuboid (top face ABCD, bottom face EFGH, vertical edges AE, BF, CG, DH of height $2$ cm), with base edges $HG=5$ cm and $GF=3$ cm. Calculate (a) the length CA (diagonal of the top face), (b) the length CE (space diagonal), (c) the angle ACE.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) The top face ABCD has the same dimensions as EFGH: $CA=\sqrt{5^2+3^2}=\sqrt{34}=5.831$ cm.

(b) $CE=\sqrt{5^2+3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{38}=6.164$ cm (the cuboid's space diagonal).

(c) In triangle ACE: $CA=5.831$, $CE=6.164$, $AE=2$ (vertical edge). By the cosine rule: $\cos(\angle ACE)=\dfrac{CA^2+CE^2-AE^2}{2\cdot CA\cdot CE}=\dfrac{34+38-4}{2(5.831)(6.164)}=0.9459 \Rightarrow \angle ACE=18.932°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In a cuboid ABCDEFGH (top face ABCD, bottom face EFGH, vertical edges of height $12$ cm), the base edges are $HG=4$ cm and $GF=5$ cm. Calculate (a) the length EG, (b) the length AG, (c) the angle AGE.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $EG=\sqrt{4^2+5^2}=\sqrt{41}=6.403$ cm.

(b) $AG=\sqrt{EG^2+AE^2}=\sqrt{41+144}=\sqrt{185}=13.601$ cm.

(c) Triangle AGE is right-angled at E (AE vertical, EG horizontal): $\tan(\angle AGE)=\dfrac{AE}{EG}=\dfrac{12}{6.403} \Rightarrow \angle AGE=61.916°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: In a cuboid ABCDEFGH (top face ABCD, bottom face EFGH, vertical edges of height $7$ cm), the base edges are $HG=3$ cm and $GF=2$ cm. Calculate (a) the angle BCE, (b) the angle GFH.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $BC=GF=2$ cm, $CE=\sqrt{3^2+2^2+7^2}=\sqrt{62}=7.874$ cm (space diagonal), $BE=\sqrt{AB^2+AE^2}=\sqrt{3^2+7^2}=\sqrt{58}=7.616$ cm (back-face diagonal). By the cosine rule in triangle BCE: $\cos(\angle BCE)=\dfrac{BC^2+CE^2-BE^2}{2\cdot BC\cdot CE}=\dfrac{4+62-58}{2(2)(7.874)}=0.2540 \Rightarrow \angle BCE=75.286°$.

(b) In the base rectangle EFGH, angle $G=90°$. $\tan(\angle GFH)=\dfrac{GH}{GF}=\dfrac{3}{2} \Rightarrow \angle GFH=56.310°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: DEBC is the rectangular base of a right pyramid with apex A vertically above the centre X of the base ($DE=6$ cm, $EB=4$ cm). The slant edge $AB=10$ cm. Calculate (a)(i) the length DB, (ii) the angle DAX; (b)(i) the angle CED, (ii) the angle DBA.
exercises.full_solution:
(a)(i) $DB=\sqrt{6^2+4^2}=\sqrt{52}=7.211$ cm (diagonal of the rectangular base).

(ii) $BX=\tfrac12DB=3.606$ cm. In right triangle ABX (right angle at X): $AX=\sqrt{AB^2-BX^2}=\sqrt{100-13.000}=9.327$ cm. $\tan(\angle DAX)=\dfrac{DX}{AX}=\dfrac{3.606}{9.327} \Rightarrow \angle DAX=21.134°$ (since $DX=BX=3.606$ cm, both half-diagonals).

(b)(i) In the base rectangle, $\angle CED$ is the angle between edge $ED$ and diagonal $EC$: $\tan(\angle CED)=\dfrac{EB}{ED}=\dfrac46 \Rightarrow \angle CED=33.690°$.

(ii) Since the pyramid is a right pyramid, all slant edges are equal: $AD=AB=10$ cm. In isosceles triangle ABD ($AB=AD=10$, $BD=7.211$): $\cos(\angle DBA)=\dfrac{AB^2+BD^2-AD^2}{2\cdot AB\cdot BD}=\dfrac{100+52-100}{2(10)(7.211)}=0.3606 \Rightarrow \angle DBA=68.866°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: DEBC is the rectangular base of a right pyramid with apex A vertically above the centre X of the base ($DE=8$ cm, $EB=3$ cm). The slant edge $AB=9$ cm. Calculate (a)(i) the length CE, (ii) the angle CAX; (b)(i) the angle BDE, (ii) the angle ADB.
exercises.full_solution:
(a)(i) $CE=\sqrt{8^2+3^2}=\sqrt{73}=8.544$ cm.

(ii) All slant edges of a right pyramid are equal, so $AC=AB=9$ cm. $CX=\tfrac12CE=4.272$ cm. $AX=\sqrt{AC^2-CX^2}=\sqrt{81-18.250}=7.921$ cm. $\tan(\angle CAX)=\dfrac{CX}{AX}=\dfrac{4.272}{7.921} \Rightarrow \angle CAX=28.338°$.

(b)(i) $\tan(\angle BDE)=\dfrac{EB}{DE}=\dfrac38 \Rightarrow \angle BDE=20.556°$ (angle between base edge DE and diagonal DB).

(ii) All slant edges equal: $AD=AB=9$ cm. In isosceles triangle ADB ($AD=AB=9$, $DB=8.544$): $\cos(\angle ADB)=\dfrac{AD^2+DB^2-AB^2}{2\cdot AD\cdot DB}=\dfrac{DB^2}{2(9)(8.544)}=0.4747 \Rightarrow \angle ADB=61.662°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A right circular cone has apex X. Y is the centre of the circular base and Z is a point on the circumference of the base, so XY is the vertical height and YZ is a radius. The slant height $XZ=13$ cm and angle $YXZ=60°$. Calculate (a) the length XY, (b) the length YZ, (c) the circumference of the base.
exercises.full_solution:
Triangle XYZ is right-angled at Y, because the axis XY is perpendicular to the base.

(a) $XY=13\cos60°=6.5$ cm.

(b) $YZ=13\sin60°=11.258$ cm.

(c) YZ is the radius of the base, so the circumference $=2\pi\times YZ=2\pi\times11.258=70.7$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: ABCDEFGH is a cuboid (top face ABCD, bottom face EFGH, vertical edges AE, BF, CG, DH of height $4$ cm), with base edges $HG=5$ cm and $GF=2$ cm. (a) Calculate the length EC. (b) Calculate the angle between the line CE and the plane ADHE.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) First, $EG^2=EH^2+HG^2=2^2+5^2=29 \Rightarrow EG=\sqrt{29}$ cm. Then $EC^2=EG^2+CG^2=29+16=45 \Rightarrow EC=\sqrt{45}=6.71$ cm (3 s.f.).

(b) CD is perpendicular to the plane ADHE (it is parallel to HG, which is perpendicular to that face), so the projection of C onto ADHE is D and the required angle is angle CED in triangle CDE, which is right-angled at D: $\sin E=\dfrac{CD}{CE}=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{45}} \Rightarrow E=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{45}}\right)=48.2°$ (1 d.p.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (angle between a line and a plane)

exercises.statement: A prism has vertices P, Q (back top edge), T, U (front top edge), S, R (back bottom edge, R hidden), W, V (front bottom edge), forming planes PQUT (top), RSWV (bottom), PQRS (back), TUVW (front), QRVU (right) and PSWT (left). Name the projection of each line onto the given plane: (a) TR onto RSWV (b) TR onto PQUT (c) SU onto PQRS (d) SU onto TUVW (e) PV onto QRVU (f) PV onto RSWV.
exercises.answer: (a) WR (b) TQ (c) SQ (d) WU (e) QV (f) SV
exercises.full_solution:
In each case, project the endpoint not already in the given plane straight onto it (keeping its position within the plane's two directions, changing only the coordinate normal to the plane), then join to the endpoint already in the plane:

(a) R is already in RSWV; T projects onto this (bottom) plane at W (T's front/left position, dropped to the bottom): projection = WR.

(b) T is already in PQUT; R projects onto this (top) plane at Q (R's back/right position, raised to the top): projection = TQ.

(c) S is already in PQRS (back); U projects onto the back plane at Q: projection = SQ.

(d) U is already in TUVW (front); S projects onto the front plane at W: projection = WU.

(e) V is already in QRVU (right); P projects onto the right plane at Q: projection = QV.

(f) V is already in RSWV (bottom); P projects onto the bottom plane at S: projection = SV.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cuboid has vertices H, I (back top edge), K, J (front top edge), L, M (back bottom edge, hidden), O, N (front bottom edge), forming planes IJNM (right), JKON (front), HIML (back), HLOK (left), LMNO (bottom). Name the projection of each line onto the given plane: (a) KM onto IJNM (b) KM onto JKON (c) KM onto HIML (d) IO onto HLOK (e) IO onto JKON (f) IO onto LMNO.
exercises.answer: (a) JM (b) KN (c) HM (d) HO (e) JO (f) MO
exercises.full_solution:
(a) M is already in IJNM (right); K projects onto the right plane at J: projection = JM.

(b) K is already in JKON (front); M projects onto the front plane at N: projection = KN.

(c) M is already in HIML (back); K projects onto the back plane at H: projection = HM.

(d) O is already in HLOK (left); I projects onto the left plane at H: projection = HO.

(e) O is already in JKON (front); I projects onto the front plane at J: projection = JO.

(f) O is already in LMNO (bottom); I projects onto the bottom plane at M: projection = MO.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Using the same prism as Q1 (vertices P, Q, T, U, S, R, W, V, with planes PQRS back, TUVW front, PSWT left, QRVU right, RSWV bottom, PQUT top), name the angle between the given line and plane: (a) PT and PQRS (b) PU and PQRS (c) SV and PSWT (d) RT and TUVW (e) SU and QRVU (f) PV and PSWT.
exercises.answer: (a) PT is perpendicular to PQRS, so the angle is $90°$ (T projects exactly onto P; there is no distinct named angle) (b) angle UPQ (c) angle VSW (d) angle RTV (e) angle SUR (f) angle VPW
exercises.full_solution:
(a) T projects onto the back plane PQRS at P itself (PT runs in the depth direction, perpendicular to that face), so PT ⟂ PQRS and the angle is $90°$.

(b) U projects onto PQRS at Q, so the angle between PU and its projection PQ is angle UPQ.

(c) V projects onto PSWT (left) at W, so the angle is angle VSW.

(d) R projects onto TUVW (front) at V, so the angle is angle RTV.

(e) S projects onto QRVU (right) at R, so the angle is angle SUR.

(f) P lies in PSWT and V projects onto PSWT (left) at W, so the angle is between PV and PW: angle VPW.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: ABCDEFGH is a cuboid (top ABCD, bottom EFGH, vertical edges of height $3$ cm), with base edges $HG=4$ cm and $GF=3$ cm. (a) Calculate the length BH. (b) Calculate the angle between the line BH and the plane EFGH.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Base diagonal $HF=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$ cm. $BH=\sqrt{HF^2+BF^2}=\sqrt{25+9}=\sqrt{34}=5.831$ cm.

(b) The angle between BH and the base plane EFGH is angle BHF (between BH and its projection HF): $\tan(\angle BHF)=\dfrac{BF}{HF}=\dfrac35 \Rightarrow \angle BHF=30.964°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: ABCDEFGH is a cuboid (top ABCD, bottom EFGH, vertical edges of height $5$ cm), with base edges $HG=8$ cm and $GF=4$ cm. (a) Calculate the length AG. (b) Calculate the angle between the line AG and the plane EFGH. (c) Calculate the angle between the line AG and the plane ADHE.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $EG=\sqrt{8^2+4^2}=\sqrt{80}=8.944$ cm. $AG=\sqrt{EG^2+AE^2}=\sqrt{80+25}=\sqrt{105}=10.247$ cm.

(b) The angle between AG and the base EFGH is angle AGE: $\tan(\angle AGE)=\dfrac{AE}{EG}=\dfrac{5}{8.944} \Rightarrow \angle AGE=29.206°$.

(c) Plane ADHE is the left face. A already lies on this plane; G projects onto it at H (since $GH=HG=8$ cm is measured perpendicular to this plane). The angle between AG and the plane is therefore angle GAH, measured at A between AG and its projection AH: $\sin(\angle GAH)=\dfrac{GH}{AG}=\dfrac{8}{10.247} \Rightarrow \angle GAH=51.327°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: DEBC is the rectangular base of a right pyramid with apex A vertically above the centre X ($DE=6$ cm, $EB=3$ cm). The slant edge $AB=7$ cm. (a) Calculate the length BD. (b) Calculate the angle between AB and the plane CBED (the base).
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $BD=\sqrt{6^2+3^2}=\sqrt{45}=6.708$ cm (diagonal of the base).

(b) B lies on the base plane; A projects onto the base at X (the centre), so the angle between AB and the base is angle ABX. $BX=\tfrac12BD=3.354$ cm. $\cos(\angle ABX)=\dfrac{BX}{AB}=\dfrac{3.354}{7} \Rightarrow \angle ABX=61.370°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: WVYZ is the rectangular base of a right pyramid with apex U vertically above the centre X ($ZY=6$ cm, $YV=5$ cm). The slant edge $UV=12$ cm. (a) Calculate the length WY. (b) Calculate the length UX. (c) Calculate the angle between UX and the plane UZY.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $WY=\sqrt{5^2+6^2}=\sqrt{61}=7.810$ cm (diagonal of the base).

(b) $VX=\tfrac12WY=3.905$ cm. $UX=\sqrt{UV^2-VX^2}=\sqrt{144-15.250}=11.347$ cm.

(c) Let M be the midpoint of ZY. The plane UXM is perpendicular to the edge ZY, so the projection of X onto the face UZY lies on UM, and the required angle is angle XUM. $XM=\tfrac12YV=2.5$ cm and triangle UXM is right-angled at X, so $\tan(\angle XUM)=\dfrac{XM}{UX}=\dfrac{2.5}{11.347}\Rightarrow\angle XUM=12.425°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: ABCD and EFGH are square faces of a frustum, lying parallel to each other (ABCD on top, side $10$ cm; EFGH on the bottom, side $6$ cm), with corresponding vertices joined by slant edges; $CG=8$ cm. Calculate (a) the length DB, (b) the length HF, (c) the vertical height of the object, (d) the angle DH makes with the plane ABCD.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $DB=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=\sqrt{200}=14.142$ cm.

(b) $HF=\sqrt{6^2+6^2}=\sqrt{72}=8.485$ cm.

(c) Since the frustum is symmetric about a common vertical axis, each slant edge's horizontal offset is $\tfrac12(DB-HF)=2.828$ cm; the vertical height $=\sqrt{CG^2-\text{offset}^2}=\sqrt{64-8.000}=7.483$ cm.

(d) By symmetry, DH has the same horizontal offset (2.828 cm) and vertical component (7.483 cm) as CG, so $DH=\sqrt{\text{offset}^2+h^2}=8.000$ cm (=8 cm). The angle between DH and the (horizontal) plane ABCD is $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{h}{\text{offset}}\right)=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{7.483}{2.828}\right)=69.295°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: ABCD and EFGH are square faces of a frustum, lying parallel to each other (ABCD on top, side $12$ cm; EFGH on the bottom, side $4$ cm), with corresponding vertices joined by slant edges; $CG=9$ cm. Calculate (a) the length AC, (b) the length EG, (c) the vertical height of the object, (d) the angle CG makes with the plane EFGH.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $AC=\sqrt{12^2+12^2}=\sqrt{288}=16.971$ cm.

(b) $EG=\sqrt{4^2+4^2}=\sqrt{32}=5.657$ cm.

(c) Horizontal offset $=\tfrac12(AC-EG)=5.657$ cm. Height $=\sqrt{CG^2-\text{offset}^2}=\sqrt{81-32.000}=7.000$ cm.

(d) The angle between CG and the (horizontal) plane EFGH is $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{h}{\text{offset}}\right)=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{7.000}{5.657}\right)=51.058°$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A climber at the top of Mont Blanc can see several ski resorts. Using a map she records their distance and bearing: Val d'Isère $30$ km bearing $082°$; Les Arcs $40$ km bearing $135°$; La Plagne $45$ km bearing $205°$; Méribel $35$ km bearing $320°$ (all from the climber's position). Find (a) the distance and bearing of Val d'Isère from La Plagne, (b) the distance and bearing of Méribel from Les Arcs.
mark_scheme: M1 set up coordinates for all four resorts using bearing formula
A1 correct coordinates for Val d'Isère and La Plagne
M1 vector P to V and its magnitude
A1 CAO distance (a) 66.3 km
A1 correct bearing (a) 047°
M1 vector L to M and its magnitude
A1 CAO distance (b) 74.9 km
A1 correct bearing (b) 317°
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A coastal radar station picks up a distress call from a ship $50$ km away on a bearing of $345°$. The radar station also contacts a lifeboat at sea, $20$ km away on a bearing of $220°$. Find the distance and bearing of the ship from the lifeboat.
exam_questions.full_solution:
Take the radar station as the origin. Ship $X=(50\sin345°,50\cos345°)=(-12.94,48.30)$. Lifeboat $Y=(20\sin220°,20\cos220°)=(-12.86,-15.32)$.

Vector $Y\to X = (-0.08, 63.62)$. Distance $=\sqrt{0.08^2+63.62^2}=63.6$ km (3 s.f.).

Bearing $=\tan^{-1}(-0.08/63.62) \approx 359.9°\approx 000°$ (the ship is almost due north of the lifeboat).
mark_scheme: M1 coordinates of ship X
M1 coordinates of lifeboat Y
M1 vector Y to X
A1 CAO distance 63.6 km
M1 bearing calculation
A1 bearing ≈ 000°
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: An aircraft is seen on radar at airport A. It is $210$ km away from the airport on a bearing of $065°$. The aircraft is diverted to airport B, which is $130$ km from A on a bearing of $215°$. Find the distance and bearing of airport B from the aircraft.
mark_scheme: M1 coordinates of aircraft D
M1 coordinates of airport B
M1 vector D to B and its magnitude
A1 CAO distance 329 km
M1 bearing calculation (third-quadrant vector)
A1 bearing ≈ 234°
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Calculate the length of the side marked $x$ cm in each of the following right-angled triangles: (a) hypotenuse $8$ cm, one angle $30°$, $x$ is the side opposite the $30°$ angle; (b) a right-angled triangle in which the side opposite a marked angle of $20°$ is $15$ cm, and $x$ is the hypotenuse; (c) a right-angled triangle in which the side adjacent to a marked angle of $60°$ is $10.4$ cm, and $x$ is the hypotenuse; (d) a right-angled triangle in which the side opposite a marked angle of $50°$ is $3$ cm, and $x$ is the hypotenuse.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $x=8\sin30°=4.00$ cm.

(b) $\sin20°=15/x \Rightarrow x=15/\sin20°=43.857$ cm.

(c) $\cos60°=10.4/x \Rightarrow x=10.4/\cos60°=20.8$ cm.

(d) $\sin50°=3/x \Rightarrow x=3/\sin50°=3.916$ cm.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for sinθ=opp/hyp set up, A1 for x=4 cm
(b) M1 for sin20°=15/x, A1 for x=43.9 cm (3 s.f.)
(c) M1 for cos60°=10.4/x, A1 for x=20.8 cm
(d) M1 for sin50°=3/x, A1 for x=3.92 cm (3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Calculate the size of the angle marked $\theta°$ in each of the following right-angled triangles: (a) hypotenuse $15$ cm, with the side opposite $\theta$ equal to $9$ cm; (b) the two legs of the right angle are $4.2$ cm and $6.3$ cm, with $\theta$ between the $4.2$ cm leg and the hypotenuse.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $\sin\theta=9/15=0.6 \Rightarrow \theta=\sin^{-1}(0.6)=36.870°$.

(b) $\tan\theta=6.3/4.2=1.5 \Rightarrow \theta=\tan^{-1}(1.5)=56.310°$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for sinθ=9/15, A1 for θ=36.9° (3 s.f.)
(b) M1 for tanθ=6.3/4.2, A1 for θ=56.3° (3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A map shows three towns A, B and C. Town A is due north of C. Town B is due east of A. The distance AC is $75$ km and the bearing of C from B is $245°$. Calculate, giving your answers to the nearest $100$ m: (a) the distance AB, (b) the distance BC.
exam_questions.full_solution:
Place A at the origin. C is due south of A with $AC=75$ km, and B is due east of A, so angle $BAC=90°$.

The bearing of C from B is $245°$. The direction from B back to A is due west (bearing $270°$), so angle $ABC=270°-245°=25°$ (equivalently, angle $ACB=65°$).

(a) In right-angled triangle ABC (right angle at A): $\tan25°=\dfrac{AC}{AB}$, so $AB=\dfrac{75}{\tan25°}=160.838$ km $=160.8$ km (nearest 100 m).

(b) $\sin25°=\dfrac{AC}{BC}$, so $BC=\dfrac{75}{\sin25°}=177.465$ km $=177.5$ km (nearest 100 m).
mark_scheme: M1 for recognising angle A = 90° (AC north-south, AB east-west)
M1 for angle ABC = 25° (or angle ACB = 65°) from the bearing, with a correct ratio such as tan25° = 75/AB
A1 for AB = 160.8 km (nearest 100 m: 160.8 km)
M1 for BC = 75/sin25° (or Pythagoras with AB and AC)
A1 for BC = 177.5 km (nearest 100 m)
B1 for correct to stated accuracy (nearest 100 m) throughout
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Two trees stand $16$ m apart. Their tops make an angle of $\theta°$ at point A on the ground; A, and the tops of both trees, are collinear (the line of sight from A grazes the top of the shorter tree and continues to the top of the taller tree). The shorter tree has height $5$ m and is $x$ m from A; the taller tree has height $7.5$ m. (a) Express $\theta°$ in terms of the height of the shorter tree and $x$. (b) Express $\theta°$ in terms of the height of the taller tree and its distance from A. (c) Form an equation in terms of $x$. (d) Calculate the value of $x$. (e) Calculate the value of $\theta$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) In the right triangle formed with the shorter tree: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{x}$.

(b) The taller tree is $x+16$ m from A (it stands $16$ m beyond the shorter tree): $\tan\theta=\dfrac{7.5}{x+16}$.

(c) Since both expressions equal $\tan\theta$: $\dfrac{5}{x}=\dfrac{7.5}{x+16}$.

(d) Cross-multiplying: $5(x+16)=7.5x \Rightarrow 5x+80=7.5x \Rightarrow 80=2.5x \Rightarrow x=32$ m.

(e) $\theta=\tan^{-1}(5/32)=8.881°$.
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for tanθ = 5/x
(b) B1 for tanθ = 7.5/(x+16)
(c) M1 for equating the two expressions for tanθ
(d) M1 for cross-multiplying and solving the linear equation, A1 for x = 32 m
(e) M1 for θ = tan⁻¹(5/32), A1 for θ = 8.88° (3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Two boats X and Y, sailing in a race, are shown in a diagram. Boat X is $145$ m due north of a buoy B. Boat Y is due east of buoy B. Boats X and Y are $320$ m apart. Calculate (a) the distance BY, (b) the bearing of Y from X, (c) the bearing of X from Y.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) Triangle XBY has a right angle at B (XB is vertical/north-south, BY is horizontal/east-west). By Pythagoras: $BY=\sqrt{320^2-145^2}=\sqrt{81375}=285.263$ m.

(b) From X, Y lies to the south-east: the angle between south (at X) and XY is $\tan^{-1}(BY/145)=\tan^{-1}(285.263/145)=63.056°$. So the bearing of Y from X $=180°-63.056°=116.944°$.

(c) The bearing of X from Y is the back bearing: $=116.944°+180°=296.944°$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for Pythagoras BY²=320²-145², A1 for BY = 285 m (3 s.f.)
(b) M1 for correct right-triangle angle calculation, A1 for bearing = 116.9° (1 d.p.)
(c) M1 for back bearing = bearing + 180°, A1 for bearing = 296.9° (1 d.p.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Two hawks P and Q are flying vertically above one another (P below Q). Hawk Q is $250$ m above hawk P. They both spot a snake at R on the ground. The horizontal distance from R to the point on the ground directly below P and Q is $2.8$ km, and the angle of elevation of P from R is $35°$. Using the information given, calculate (a) the height of P above the ground, (b) the distance between P and R, (c) the distance between Q and R.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $\tan35°=\dfrac{\text{height of P}}{2800} \Rightarrow \text{height of P}=2800\tan35°=1960.58$ m.

(b) $\cos35°=\dfrac{2800}{PR} \Rightarrow PR=\dfrac{2800}{\cos35°}=3418.17$ m.

(c) Height of Q $=$ height of P $+250=2210.58$ m. By Pythagoras, $QR=\sqrt{2800^2+2210.58^2}=3567.45$ m.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for tan35° = height(P)/2800, A1 for height(P) = 1961 m (nearest m)
(b) M1 for cos35° = 2800/PR, A1 for PR = 3418 m (nearest m)
(c) M1 for height(Q) = height(P)+250, M1 for Pythagoras with 2800 and height(Q), A1 for QR = 3567 m (nearest m, final answer dependent on part (a))
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Solve the following trigonometric equations, giving all the solutions in the range $0\le x\le360$: (a) $\sin x=\dfrac25$ (b) $\tan x=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$ (c) $\cos x=-0.1$ (d) $\sin x=1$.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $x=\sin^{-1}(0.4)=23.578°$; other solution $=180-23.578=156.422°$.

(b) $-\sqrt3/3=-1/\sqrt3$; reference angle $=\tan^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)=30°$; tangent negative in 2nd/4th quadrants: $x=180-30=150°$, $x=360-30=330°$.

(c) $x=\cos^{-1}(-0.1)=95.739°$. Cosine is negative in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants, and the cosine curve is symmetrical about $x=180°$, so the second solution is $360-95.739=264.261°$.

(d) $\sin x=1$ only at the single maximum point in this range: $x=90°$.
mark_scheme: (b) M1 for reference angle 30° and correct quadrants, A1 for x = 150°, 330°
(d) B1 for x = 90° only
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Explain, with the aid of a graph, why the equation $\cos x=\dfrac32$ has no solutions.
exam_questions.answer: No solutions exist because $\cos x$ can never exceed $1$.
exam_questions.full_solution: The graph of $y=\cos x$ oscillates between a minimum of $-1$ and a maximum of $1$ for all $x$. Since $\dfrac32=1.5>1$, the horizontal line $y=1.5$ never intersects the cosine curve, so there is no value of $x$ for which $\cos x=1.5$. The equation therefore has no solutions.
mark_scheme: M1 for stating the range of cosine is [-1,1] (with reference to the graph)
A1 for concluding no solutions since 3/2 lies outside this range
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: The cosine of which other angle between $0°$ and $180°$ has the same value as: (a) $\cos128°$ (b) $-\cos80°$?
exam_questions.full_solution: Using $\cos x°=-\cos(180-x)°$: (a) $\cos128°=-\cos(180-128)°=-\cos52°$, so the paired angle is $52°$. (b) $-\cos80°=\cos(180-80)°=\cos100°$, so the angle is $100°$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for applying the identity, A1 for 52°
(b) M1 for applying the identity, A1 for 100°
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A circle of radius $3$ cm, centre O, is shown on a pair of coordinate axes. The points A and B lie where the circumference of the circle intersects the $x$-axis (so $A=(-3,0)$, $B=(3,0)$). Point C is free to move on the circumference. (a) Deduce, justifying your answer, the size of angle ACB. (b) If $BC=3$ cm, calculate the possible coordinates of point C, giving your answers in exact form.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\angle ACB=90°$ for any position of C (b) $C=\left(\dfrac32,\ \dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ or $C=\left(\dfrac32,\ -\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right)$
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) AB is a diameter of the circle (length $6$ cm, passing through the centre O). By the circle theorem 'the angle in a semicircle is $90°$' (angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference is a right angle), $\angle ACB=90°$ for any position of C on the circle (except at A or B themselves).

(b) Let $C=(x,y)$. Since C lies on the circle: $x^2+y^2=9$. Since $BC=3$ and $B=(3,0)$: $(x-3)^2+y^2=9$. Subtracting the first equation from the second: $(x-3)^2-x^2=0 \Rightarrow -6x+9=0 \Rightarrow x=\dfrac32$. Then $y^2=9-\dfrac94=\dfrac{27}{4} \Rightarrow y=\pm\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}$. So $C=\left(\dfrac32,\pm\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right)$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for identifying AB as a diameter, A1 for angle ACB = 90° with correct circle-theorem justification
(b) M1 for setting up x²+y²=9 and (x-3)²+y²=9, M1 for solving simultaneously, A1 for x=3/2, A1 for y=±3√3/2 (both coordinate pairs given)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Triangle PQR has $PQ=8$ cm, $PR=7$ cm, and angle $PQR=40°$. (a) Calculate the two possible values for angle PRQ. (b) Calculate the shortest distance possible of R from side PQ.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\angle PRQ\approx47.3°$ or $132.7°$ (b) shortest possible distance $\approx0.886$ cm
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) By the sine rule: $\dfrac{PQ}{\sin(\angle PRQ)}=\dfrac{PR}{\sin(\angle PQR)} \Rightarrow \sin(\angle PRQ)=\dfrac{8\sin40°}{7}=0.7346 \Rightarrow \angle PRQ=47.27°$ or $180-47.27=132.73°$.

(b) For each case, angle $P=180-40-\angle PRQ$: case 1, $P=92.73°$, height $=PR\sin P=7\sin(92.73°)=6.992$ cm; case 2, $P=7.27°$, height $=7\sin(7.27°)=0.886$ cm. The shortest distance possible (the smaller of the two valid configurations) is $0.886$ cm.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for correct sine rule set-up, A1 for 47.3°, A1 for 132.7°
(b) M1 for finding angle P in at least one case, M1 for height = PR sin P, A1 for identifying and giving the shorter distance (0.886 cm, 3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A triangle has two sides of $18$ cm and $26$ cm. The angle opposite the $18$ cm side is $30°$. Calculate the size of the obtuse angle (marked $\theta°$) opposite the $26$ cm side.
exam_questions.full_solution: By the sine rule: $\dfrac{18}{\sin30°}=\dfrac{26}{\sin\theta} \Rightarrow \sin\theta=\dfrac{26\sin30°}{18}=0.7222 \Rightarrow \theta=46.24°$ or $180-46.24=133.76°$. Since $\theta$ is specified to be obtuse, $\theta=133.76°$.
mark_scheme: M1 for correct sine rule set-up
M1 for finding the reference angle (46.2°)
A1 for the obtuse angle 133.8° (1 d.p.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: ABCDEFGH is a cuboid (top ABCD, bottom EFGH, vertical edges of height $4$ cm), with base edges $HG=10$ cm and $GF=6$ cm. Calculate (a) the length EG, (b) the length EC, (c) the angle BEC.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $EG=\sqrt{10^2+6^2}=\sqrt{136}=11.662$ cm.

(b) $EC=\sqrt{10^2+6^2+4^2}=\sqrt{152}=12.329$ cm.

(c) $EB=\sqrt{10^2+4^2}=\sqrt{116}=10.770$ cm (diagonal of the back face), $BC=GF=6$ cm. By the cosine rule in triangle BEC: $\cos(\angle BEC)=\dfrac{EB^2+EC^2-BC^2}{2\cdot EB\cdot EC}=\dfrac{116+152-36}{2(10.770)(12.329)}=0.8736 \Rightarrow \angle BEC=29.122°$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for Pythagoras, A1 for EG = 11.7 cm (3 s.f.)
(b) M1 for Pythagoras (3D), A1 for EC = 12.3 cm (3 s.f.)
(c) M1 for identifying EB and BC, M1 for correct cosine rule, A1 for angle BEC = 29.1° (3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: JKLM is a quadrilateral with $JK=25$ m, $KL=12$ m, $LM=20$ m, angle $J$ (full angle $KJM$) $=70°$, and angle $K=42°$. The diagonal JL is drawn. Calculate (a) the length JL, (b) angle KJL, (c) the length JM, (d) the area of JKLM.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) In triangle JKL: $JL^2=25^2+12^2-2(25)(12)\cos42°=769-600(0.7431)=323.11 \Rightarrow JL=17.975$ m.

(b) By the sine rule: $\sin(\angle KJL)=\dfrac{KL\sin42°}{JL}=\dfrac{12\sin42°}{17.975}=0.4467 \Rightarrow \angle KJL=26.532°$.

(c) $\angle LJM=70°-\angle KJL=43.468°$. In triangle JLM, by the sine rule: $\sin(\angle JML)=\dfrac{JL\sin(\angle LJM)}{LM}=\dfrac{17.975\sin43.468°}{20}=0.6183 \Rightarrow \angle JML=38.192°$ (the obtuse alternative $141.8°$ is impossible, because $141.8°+43.5°>180°$). Then $\angle JLM=180-43.468-38.192=98.340°$, and $JM=\dfrac{LM\sin(\angle JLM)}{\sin(\angle LJM)}=\dfrac{20\sin98.340°}{\sin43.468°}=28.765$ m.

(d) Area $=\tfrac12(JK)(KL)\sin42°+\tfrac12(JL)(JM)\sin(\angle LJM)=\tfrac12(25)(12)\sin42°+\tfrac12(17.975)(28.765)\sin(43.468°)=100.370+177.853=278.22$ m$^2$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for cosine rule set-up, A1 for JL = 18.0 m (3 s.f.)
(b) M1 for sine rule, A1 for angle KJL = 26.5° (3 s.f.)
(c) M1 for angle LJM = 43.5°, M1 for solving for JM, A1 for JM = 28.8 m (3 s.f.)
(d) M1 for area = sum of the two triangles' areas, A1 for total area ≈ 278 m² (3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A square-based right pyramid has base edge $9$ cm (so $BE=DE=9$ cm) and slant edge $AD=16$ cm (all slant edges equal). Calculate (a) the length BD, (b) angle ABD, (c) the area of triangle ABD, (d) the vertical height of the pyramid.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $BD=\sqrt{162}=12.728$ cm (b) $\angle ABD\approx66.56°$ (c) area $\approx93.42$ cm$^2$ (d) height $\approx14.68$ cm
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) $BD=\sqrt{9^2+9^2}=\sqrt{162}=12.728$ cm.

(b) All slant edges are equal: $AB=AD=16$ cm. Triangle ABD is isosceles with base $BD=12.728$ cm. $\cos(\angle ABD)=\dfrac{AB^2+BD^2-AD^2}{2\cdot AB\cdot BD}=\dfrac{BD^2}{2(16)(12.728)}=0.3977 \Rightarrow \angle ABD=66.563°$.

(c) Angle at apex $A=180-2(66.563)=46.875°$. Area $=\tfrac12(AB)(AD)\sin A=\tfrac12(16)(16)\sin(46.875°)=93.422$ cm$^2$.

(d) $BX=\tfrac12BD=6.364$ cm (X = centre of base). Height $=\sqrt{AB^2-BX^2}=\sqrt{256-40.500}=14.680$ cm.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for Pythagoras on the square base, A1 for BD = 12.7 cm (3 s.f.)
(b) M1 for recognising AB=AD=16 (equal slant edges), M1 for cosine rule, A1 for angle ABD = 66.6° (3 s.f.)
(c) M1 for apex angle / area method, A1 for area ≈ 93.4 cm² (3 s.f.)
(d) M1 for Pythagoras using half-diagonal and slant edge, A1 for height ≈ 14.7 cm (3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Two points X and Y are $1000$ m apart on a straight piece of coastline. A buoy Z is out at sea, with $XZ=850$ m and $YZ=625$ m. A girl wishes to swim from the coast to the buoy. (a) What is the shortest distance she will have to swim (to 3 s.f.)? (b) How far along the coast from Y will she have to set off, to swim the least distance?
exam_questions.full_solution:
Set X at the origin and Y at $(1000,0)$ along the coast, with Z at $(x,h)$. Then $x^2+h^2=850^2$ and $(x-1000)^2+h^2=625^2$. Subtracting: $(x-1000)^2-x^2=625^2-850^2 \Rightarrow -2000x+1{,}000{,}000=625^2-850^2 \Rightarrow x=\dfrac{850^2-625^2+1000^2}{2(1000)}=665.938$ m.

(a) The shortest swimming distance is the perpendicular distance $h=\sqrt{850^2-x^2}=\sqrt{850^2-665.938^2}=528.230$ m $\approx528$ m (3 s.f.).

(b) Distance along the coast from Y to the landing point $=1000-x=334.062$ m.
mark_scheme: M1 for setting up coordinates/equations for the perpendicular foot
M1 for solving the linear equation for x = 665.9 m (distance from X), M1 for h = √(850² − x²)
A1 for the shortest distance ≈ 528 m (3 s.f.)
M1 for 1000 − x, A1 for the distance from Y ≈ 334 m (3 s.f.)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
